exam: Montepulciano is a grape here and a town in Tuscany: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is the grape, Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is Sangiovese; the most tested Italian trap.

Three DOCGs: Colline Teramane Montepulciano d'Abruzzo (2003), Terre Tollesi or Tullum (2019) and Casauria (2025). Casauria requires at least 90 per cent Montepulciano; Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo remains a DOC.
Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo is a deep rosato from Montepulciano; cerasa means cherry. Cerasuolo di Vittoria in Sicily is a red blend, a different wine.
Trebbiano d'Abruzzo may be Trebbiano Abruzzese or Trebbiano Toscano; the Abruzzese is the distinct, long lived vine.
Pecorino is a white grape of Abruzzo and Marche named for sheep, not the cheese; Offida DOCG in Marche shares it.
The 2023 reform: provincial sub-zones on the regional DOCs, with Superiore and Riserva reserved for them.
The tendone pergola, the Adriatic, the Gran Sasso and Majella, and the Chieti plain as the volume engine of the region.

grapes.name: Montepulciano
grapes.styles: One of the most planted reds of Italy and almost the whole of Abruzzo's red vineyard: deep colour, black cherry and plum, soft tannin and modest acidity; everyday wines by the tanker and long lived ones from a few estates.

grapes.name: Trebbiano Abruzzese
grapes.styles: The true Trebbiano of the region, a distinct vine from Trebbiano Toscano and often confused with Bombino Bianco; neutral at high yields, but from old pergolas and low crops it gives a saline, slowly evolving white that can age for decades.

grapes.name: Trebbiano Toscano
grapes.styles: Permitted in Trebbiano d'Abruzzo alongside the Abruzzese, and the source of much of the plain, crisp wine under that name.

grapes.name: Pecorino
grapes.styles: A mountain white named for the sheep that grazed its vines, rescued from near extinction in the 1980s: early ripening, high in acid and alcohol, with herbs, citrus and a mineral bite.

grapes.name: Passerina
grapes.styles: A simple, fresh white of the Adriatic hills, grown for still, sparkling and passito wines.

grapes.name: Cococciola
grapes.styles: A local white of the Chieti hills with lime and green herb flavours, now bottled on its own.

grapes.name: Sangiovese
grapes.styles: One of the reds allowed to fill up to 15 per cent of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo, and rarely used by the serious estates.

law.classification: Four regional DOCs carry the names a server meets: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo (1968), Trebbiano d'Abruzzo (1972), Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo (its own DOC since 2010, having been a style of the Montepulciano DOC before) and Abruzzo DOC (2010), which takes the varietal whites such as Pecorino and Passerina. The three DOCGs are Colline Teramane Montepulciano d'Abruzzo (2003), Terre Tollesi or Tullum around Tollo (2019), and Casauria in Pescara province, recognised in 2025. Casauria was formerly a Montepulciano d'Abruzzo sub-zone and requires at least 90 per cent Montepulciano. A reform in force from the 2023 harvest wrote provincial sub-zones into the regional DOCs, Terre di Chieti, Colline Pescaresi and Terre de L'Aquila, with Colline Teramane added for Trebbiano d'Abruzzo, and reserved the Superiore and Riserva types for wines from those sub-zones with the name printed on the label; a sub-zone Montepulciano asks at least 90 per cent of the grape.

made.viticulture: The sign of Abruzzo is the tendone, the overhead pergola that spreads a canopy at head height over the fruit; it was planted for volume, and the co-operatives of the Chieti plain still crop it heavily for the wine sold by the tanker, but the two most celebrated estates of the region keep theirs on purpose, arguing that the shade protects Montepulciano and Trebbiano from the Adriatic sun and keeps the acidity. Newer plantings are Guyot or spur pruned cordon on the hills. Montepulciano ripens late, into October, and needs the long sunny autumn the mountains guarantee; Pecorino ripens early and is picked in September at full alcohol. Altitude is the lever for freshness: the Peligna valley, Ofena and the Teramo hills give the brightest reds, the coastal plain the softest. Co-operatives founded in the 1960s and 1970s take in most of the region's grapes. The hazards are hail off the mountains, autumn rain at harvest, and a hot summer that flattens the acid of the plain. Organic farming is easy in the dry air and common.
made.winemaking: Montepulciano gives colour and tannin quickly, so most of it is fermented warm for a week or so and bottled young, sometimes after months in large oak or cement, for the soft, fruit led wine the world buys. The slow school is different: long maceration, old large casks or concrete, no fining, late release and bottles that evolve for decades, with one Teramo estate crushing by foot and bottling without filtration. Cerasuolo is Montepulciano pressed off its skins after a short maceration, or run off a red fermentation after a few hours, so it keeps a cherry colour and real tannin; the Riserva reds of the DOC take two years, three for the Colline Teramane DOCG. Trebbiano d'Abruzzo is cool fermented in steel for the quick wine; the rare long lived versions sit on their lees in old wood or cement for a year or more before bottling and are not stabilised cold. Pecorino is made reductively in steel to keep its herbal bite, and some houses give it a few months of lees. Trebbiano is also dried for a small amount of passito.

places.name: Colline Teramane
places.note: The hills of Teramo province in the north, between the Gran Sasso and the sea, the region's first DOCG for Montepulciano and the home of its slowest, longest lived reds; Torano Nuovo and Controguerra are the villages that carry the names of the estates.

places.name: Controguerra
places.note: A village on the Marche border that long carried a small DOC of its own; the Pepe estate's Torano Nuovo lies beside it.

places.name: Colline Pescaresi and Loreto Aprutino
places.note: The hills behind Pescara, where Loreto Aprutino holds the vineyards of Valentini and the region's most famous Trebbiano; a provincial sub-zone of the regional DOCs since 2023.

places.name: Chieti province
places.note: The southern half of the coast and the hills behind it, home to the bulk of the vineyard, the big co-operatives, the Tullum DOCG around Tollo and San Martino sulla Marrucina, Masciarelli's village; Terre di Chieti is its sub-zone name.

places.name: Tollo
places.note: The commune of the Tullum DOCG, raised in 2019 from the Terre Tollesi DOC, for Montepulciano reds and Pecorino and Passerina whites.

places.name: L'Aquila province, the Peligna valley and Ofena
places.note: The high interior west of the Majella: the Peligna basin around Sulmona and the plateau of Ofena under the Gran Sasso, where Montepulciano and Pecorino keep acidity through cold nights; Terre de L'Aquila is the sub-zone name.

places.name: Marche, the neighbour to the north
places.note: The sheet carries no Marche locator, so its wines sit here. Verdicchio is the grape: Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi in the hills behind Ancona and the higher, inland Verdicchio di Matelica, with the Riserva of each a DOCG since 2010. Conero DOCG is Montepulciano on the limestone headland above Ancona, Rosso Piceno blends it with Sangiovese, Offida DOCG holds Pecorino and Passerina, and Lacrima di Morro d'Alba is a rose scented red.

places.name: Molise, the neighbour to the south
places.note: A small region between Abruzzo and Puglia with Biferno DOC for Montepulciano and Aglianico reds and Tintilia del Molise DOC for its own native red.

places.name: Casauria
places.note: An inland Pescara area including Castiglione a Casauria, Tocco da Casauria and neighbouring municipalities. Formerly a sub-zone of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo, it became a separate DOCG in 2025. The zone includes whole municipalities and parts of others, so town locations are orientation points rather than its boundaries.

producers.name: Valentini
producers.why: The Loreto Aprutino estate whose Trebbiano d'Abruzzo and Montepulciano, made from old pergolas and sold only in the vintages the house accepts, are the proof that both grapes can be great.

producers.name: Emidio Pepe
producers.why: Torano Nuovo in the Colline Teramane: foot crushed, unfiltered Montepulciano and Trebbiano released after years in the cellar and decanted off their sediment before sale.

producers.name: Masciarelli
producers.why: San Martino sulla Marrucina, founded 1981: the estate that took modern, polished Montepulciano d'Abruzzo abroad, with Villa Gemma as its top bottling.

producers.name: Tiberio
producers.why: A Cugnoli estate in the Pescara hills known for a pure Trebbiano Abruzzese from a single old vineyard and for crisp Pecorino and Cerasuolo.

producers.name: Cataldi Madonna
producers.why: The reference estate of Ofena on the high L'Aquila plateau, known for its Pecorino and for Montepulciano that stays fresh.

producers.name: Illuminati
producers.why: A Controguerra house of 1890 and a founder of the Colline Teramane DOCG, with Zanna as its long aged Montepulciano.

producers.name: Torre dei Beati
producers.why: An organic Loreto Aprutino estate making deep Cerasuolo and single vineyard Montepulciano from the Pescara hills.

producers.name: Praesidium
producers.why: A small Prezza estate in the Peligna valley whose mountain grown Montepulciano shows the freshness of altitude.

producers.name: Cantina Tollo
producers.why: One of the large co-operatives of the Chieti hills, founded 1960, that bottle most of the region's reliable everyday Montepulciano.

terroir.climate: Two climates in one region. The coastal hills are Mediterranean, warm and dry with sea breezes off the Adriatic; the inland valleys and the Peligna basin are continental, with cold winters, late frost and a wide day to night swing. The Apennines, here at their highest, hold back the Tyrrhenian weather, so the growing season is sunny and the autumn long enough to ripen a late grape like Montepulciano fully.
terroir.soils: Calcareous clay is the common ground, heavy on the Chieti plain and lighter in the Teramo hills. River valleys cut down to the sea with gravel and sand on their terraces. The Peligna valley and the high plateau of Ofena around L'Aquila sit on limestone scree and stony clay at altitude, which is where the freshest Montepulciano is grown.
terroir.topography: Mountains take most of the region: the Gran Sasso and the Majella rise close to 3,000 metres within 50 kilometres of the sea. Between them and the coast lie rolling hills, and the vineyards sit there, mostly below 500 metres, with the Peligna basin and the Ofena plateau higher in the interior. The Chieti province alone holds most of the vines.
terroir.water: The Adriatic gives the breezes and the humidity; the Pescara, Sangro, Vomano, Tordino and Tronto rivers run short, steep courses from the mountains to the sea and mark the vineyard valleys.

traps: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is a grape wine; Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is Sangiovese from a Tuscan town. Never let the shared word join them.
Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo is a rosato; Cerasuolo di Vittoria is a Sicilian red DOCG. Same word, two colours.
Trebbiano Abruzzese is not Trebbiano Toscano, though the DOC allows both; neither is Bombino Bianco, despite decades of confusion.
Pecorino the grape and pecorino the cheese share a shepherd, not a flavour.
Colline Teramane is a DOCG inside the Montepulciano d'Abruzzo name; the plain DOC and the DOCG are two tiers of one wine, not two wines.
Abruzzo's Riserva clock is two years for the DOC and three for Colline Teramane; do not carry Brunello's five years here.
The reform of 2023 left the plain DOC at 85 per cent Montepulciano; only the sub-zone wines ask 90.

wines.note: Deep purple, black cherry, plum and a touch of earth, with soft tannin and gentle acidity; the most reliable value red in Italy at the everyday end, and a slow, savoury, long lived wine from the Teramo and Pescara hills. Lamb arrosticini, sausages, aubergine and pasta alla chitarra.
The DOCG from the hills around Teramo: fuller structure and firmer tannin than the plain DOC, with a Riserva that spends three years in the cellar. Roast lamb, braised beef, aged pecorino.

A rosato of cherry red depth, far darker than Provence, from Montepulciano left on its skins for hours rather than days: wild strawberry, sour cherry and an almond bitterness, dry and vinous enough for grilled meat and fish stews.

Usually a light, lemony white for seafood; from the rare estates that farm old pergolas and bottle without hurry it becomes waxy, saline and nutty and lives for twenty years. Served cool, not ice cold, with brodetto and fried fish.

Taut and herbal, with lemon, thyme and a stony finish and often fourteen per cent alcohol from its early ripening; sold as Abruzzo DOC or under an IGT. Grilled fish, pecorino cheese and the region's saffron dishes.
The small DOCG around Tollo in the Chieti hills: Montepulciano reds with a Riserva, and Pecorino and Passerina whites under the same name. A local wine worth knowing for its 2019 promotion.

exam: Place both regions: Basilicata the instep between Campania and Puglia, with short Tyrrhenian and Ionian coasts; Calabria the toe between the Tyrrhenian and Ionian seas.
Tie Aglianico del Vulture to Basilicata, not Campania: Aglianico on the extinct Monte Vulture volcano, on tuff and ash.
Know Aglianico del Vulture Superiore as Basilicata's DOCG, of 2010; the plain Aglianico del Vulture stays DOC, of 1971.
Know Cirò as Calabria's Gaglioppo red of the Ionian coast, and Cirò Classico as the region's first DOCG, registered in 2025.
Know Greco di Bianco as a sweet wine from dried grapes at the toe of Calabria, not Campania's dry Greco di Tufo.
Read Superiore and Riserva as each denomination defines them: on Aglianico del Vulture, Superiore names the DOCG tier, with higher alcohol and longer ageing, and Riserva longer ageing again.
Know the climate: Mediterranean on the coasts, cooler and continental high on Vulture; decant a young Aglianico del Vulture.
The Superiore's and the Riserva's ageing years, Melissa, Savuto and Matera are asked from Premier Cru; Cirò's claim to the ancient Krimisa from Grand Cru.

grapes.name: Aglianico
grapes.styles: Basilicata's great red: late ripening, high in acid and firm in tannin, with black cherry, smoke and earth from Vulture's volcanic slopes; it needs years in cellar and bottle.

grapes.name: Gaglioppo
grapes.styles: Calabria's main red, the grape of Cirò: pale in colour but firm in tannin and often high in alcohol, with red cherry, dried herbs and spice; also rosato.

grapes.name: Magliocco
grapes.styles: A darker, softer Calabrian red, leading many wines of the Cosenza hills and the Tyrrhenian side and blended with Gaglioppo for colour and roundness.

grapes.name: Greco Bianco
grapes.styles: Calabria's name for the white of Cirò Bianco and of the sweet Greco di Bianco; a different vine from the Greco of Campania's Greco di Tufo.

grapes.name: Greco Nero
grapes.styles: A Calabrian red allowed beside Gaglioppo in Cirò, giving colour and fruit.

grapes.name: Mantonico
grapes.styles: Mantonico Bianco, an old Calabrian white made dry or as a sweet wine from dried grapes around Bianco.

grapes.name: Malvasia
grapes.styles: Malvasia Bianca di Basilicata and other Malvasias for whites under the Matera DOC and IGT Basilicata.

grapes.name: Zinfandel
grapes.styles: Grown as Primitivo in the province of Matera, for ripe, plummy reds under the Matera DOC.

law.classification: Each region now has one DOCG beside a short list of DOCs and IGTs. Basilicata's is Aglianico del Vulture Superiore, promoted in 2010 from the Aglianico del Vulture DOC of 1971: wholly Aglianico, at least 13.5 per cent alcohol and three years of ageing, five for the Riserva. The DOC continues for the younger wine, and Matera, Terre dell'Alta Val d'Agri and Grottino di Roccanova are the region's other DOCs, with IGT Basilicata covering the rest. Calabria had no DOCG until 2025, when the European Union registered Cirò Classico: a red of at least 90 per cent Gaglioppo, with Magliocco or Greco Nero, from the communes of Cirò and Cirò Marina, aged at least three years. The Cirò DOC of 1969 continues for reds and rosés of at least 80 per cent Gaglioppo and whites of at least 80 per cent Greco Bianco. Melissa, Savuto, Lamezia, Bivongi, Scavigna, Greco di Bianco and Terre di Cosenza are among Calabria's other DOCs, with IGT Calabria the broad tier.

made.viticulture: Old vineyards in both regions are bush vines, alberello, which shade their own fruit in the heat; newer plantings are on wires, trained to spurred cordon or Guyot. On Vulture, Aglianico buds early and ripens late, so the harvest runs into late October and often November, and the free draining volcanic soil and the cool nights keep the grapes healthy and fresh through the long season; spring frost and autumn rain are the risks. Calabria's coastal vineyards face the opposite problem: heat and drought, met by bush training, picking early enough to hold acidity and, in newer vineyards, some irrigation. Much of both regions is still farmed in small plots by hand, and many old vineyards were abandoned in the twentieth century as people left the south. Growers and research collections in Calabria have rescued old local grapes such as Magliocco and Mantonico from neglect.
made.winemaking: Aglianico is made as a slow red: long maceration to extract and begin taming its tannin, then ageing in large casks of oak or chestnut by the traditional cellars and in barrique by the modern ones. The Superiore must spend at least twelve months in wood and twelve in bottle within its three years. The cellars of Barile and Rionero in Vulture are cut into the soft tuff, cool and damp all year. Cirò is traditionally fermented in cement or steel and aged in large old wood, giving a pale, savoury, tannic wine; the DOCG requires three years of ageing with at least six months in wood. Rosato is made from Gaglioppo with a short maceration. Greco di Bianco is made from grapes dried after picking until they shrivel and concentrate their sugar, then pressed and fermented into a sweet wine, a method shared with the sweet Mantonico.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean on the coasts: long, hot, dry summers and mild winters, with breezes off two seas. Inland the mountains change everything. On Monte Vulture in northern Basilicata the vineyards sit high enough for cold, snowy winters, a late spring and a wide swing between hot days and cool nights, so Aglianico ripens slowly and keeps its acidity. Calabria's coastal hills are hot and dry, the heat eased by sea air by day and by cool air falling from the mountains at night; the Sila and the Aspromonte above them take rain and snow in winter.
terroir.soils: Vulture's slopes are volcanic: layers of tuff, ash and lapilli over clay, free draining and rich in minerals, soft enough for cellars to be dug into them. Elsewhere in Basilicata the hills are clay, limestone and sand. Calabria's mountains are old crystalline rock, granite, gneiss and schist in the Sila, the Serre and the Aspromonte, while its coastal hills, Cirò among them, are clay, marl, sand and limestone.
terroir.topography: Basilicata is almost all mountain and hill, the southern Apennines, with two short coasts: a short stretch on the Tyrrhenian at Maratea and the plain of Metaponto on the Ionian. Monte Vulture rises alone in the north, near the borders with Campania and Puglia, and the vineyards climb its eastern and southern slopes. Calabria is a long, narrow peninsula of mountains that fall steeply to the sea on both sides, the Pollino in the north, the Sila plateau, the Serre and the Aspromonte at the toe, with little flat land; vines grow on the coastal hills and in the river valleys.
terroir.water: The Tyrrhenian Sea washes Calabria's west coast and Basilicata's short shore at Maratea; the Ionian Sea washes Calabria's east coast, where Cirò lies, and Basilicata's Metaponto plain. The Strait of Messina parts the toe from Sicily. Two lakes fill old craters on Vulture at Monticchio, and the Ofanto river passes to the north of the volcano.

traps: Aglianico del Vulture is Basilicata's; Taurasi is Campania's Aglianico. Same grape, two regions.
Only the Superiore of Aglianico del Vulture is DOCG; the plain wine remains DOC.
Calabria had no DOCG until Cirò Classico in 2025; older books say it has none.
Cirò Classico DOCG is red only; Cirò's whites and rosés stay DOC.
Greco di Bianco is a sweet wine from a different vine than the dry Greco di Tufo of Campania.
Gaglioppo is pale but tannic and warm; its light colour is no guide to its weight.
Monte Vulture is extinct; Etna and Vesuvius are active volcanoes with vineyards on their slopes.

wines.note: Deep and firm: black cherry, plum, smoke, tar and dried herbs, high acidity and strong tannin that need years to soften. Decant a young bottle and serve it with lamb, game or aged pecorino.
The DOC wine, released younger: dark fruit, earth and volcanic smoke with firm tannin; for grilled meats, sausages and pasta with a meat ragù.

Pale garnet but firm and warm: red cherry, orange peel, dried herbs and spice, with more tannin than its colour suggests. Serve it with grilled meats, spicy salami and the chilli of Calabrian cooking.
Gaglioppo made pink: dry, with red berries and herbs and enough grip for fish soups, grilled swordfish and summer vegetables.
Greco Bianco from the Ionian coast: fresh, with citrus, white flowers and almond, a glass for seafood and raw fish.
A golden to amber sweet wine from dried grapes: apricot, candied orange, honey and almond with a fresh finish. Pour it with almond pastries or blue cheese.

exam: Taurasi: Aglianico at least 85 per cent, three years of ageing with one in wood, Riserva four with eighteen months; DOC 1970, DOCG 1993, the first DOCG in southern Italy.
Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo: both DOCG since 2003, both 85 per cent, both in Irpinia; Fiano waxy and nutty, Greco taut and flinty; Apianum on a Fiano label.
Aglianico del Taburno is Campania's fourth DOCG (2011), in the Sannio; Aglianico del Vulture is Basilicata, with its Superiore DOCG of 2010.
Lacryma Christi del Vesuvio: Vesuvio DOC, Piedirosso red, Coda di Volpe or Caprettone white, ungrafted vines on ash.
Falanghina as the region's everyday white, Falanghina del Sannio DOC and the Campi Flegrei; Piedirosso as Per' e Palummo.
The geography: Irpinia high and cold inland of Naples, harvest into November; the volcanic soils of Vesuvius, Campi Flegrei and Roccamonfina.
The house that saved the grapes after phylloxera and war, and the 1980s and 1990s estates that modernised the region.
Costa d'Amalfi's three sub-zones, Ischia's Biancolella, and Falerno del Massico as the heir of Roman Falernian.

grapes.name: Aglianico
grapes.styles: The great red of the south, late ripening, high in acid and hard in tannin, with black cherry, smoke, tar and dried herbs; Taurasi in Irpinia, Taburno in the Sannio, and the Vulture across the border in Basilicata.

grapes.name: Fiano
grapes.styles: Fiano di Avellino: waxy, hazelnut and honeysuckle with pear and smoke, fresh acidity and real weight, and a white that gains honey and toast over a decade; also grown on the coast and in Puglia.

grapes.name: Greco
grapes.styles: Greco di Tufo: taut, stony and high in acid with stone fruit, bitter almond and a flinty edge that growers credit to the sulphur rich ground of Tufo; it ages well but opens sooner than Fiano. A different vine from Calabria's Greco Bianco.

grapes.name: Falanghina
grapes.styles: The fresh white of the Sannio and the Campi Flegrei, two distinct varieties under one name: citrus, green apple and white flowers, unoaked, the region's workhorse white, also made sparkling.

grapes.name: Piedirosso
grapes.styles: Per' e Palummo, dove's foot, for its red stems: the light, peppery red of Vesuvius, the Campi Flegrei and Ischia, soft in tannin and best young.

grapes.name: Coda di Volpe
grapes.styles: Fox's tail, for its long bunch: the white of the Vesuvius slopes in Lacryma Christi Bianco, where the local Caprettone was long confused with it, and a minor partner in Irpinia's whites.

grapes.name: Biancolella
grapes.styles: Ischia's own white, with Forastera, grown on terraces over the sea for lean, saline wines.

grapes.name: Pallagrello
grapes.styles: Pallagrello Bianco and Nero, Bourbon court vines of the Caserta hills revived in the 1990s alongside Casavecchia.

law.classification: Campania holds four DOCGs, three of them in Irpinia: Taurasi, a DOC in 1970 and in 1993 the first DOCG in the south of Italy; Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo, both DOCGs since 2003; and Aglianico del Taburno in the Sannio, promoted in 2011. Irpinia DOC (2005) is the wider umbrella for the province's other wines and its Campi Taurasini sub-zone for younger Aglianico. On the coast and the bay sit the DOCs of Vesuvio with Lacryma Christi, Campi Flegrei, Ischia, Capri, Penisola Sorrentina with Gragnano, and Costa d'Amalfi with its three sub-zones of Furore, Ravello and Tramonti. To the north are Falerno del Massico, Roman Falernian's heir, Galluccio, Aversa for Asprinio and Casavecchia di Pontelatone; the Sannio holds Sannio DOC and Falanghina del Sannio DOC; Cilento covers the south. The IGTs include Campania, Beneventano, Paestum, Colli di Salerno and Terre del Volturno.
labels: the Latin name printed on Fiano di Avellino, from apis, the bee, said to have loved the grape's sweetness
tears of Christ: the Vesuvio DOC's traditional name for its red, white and rosato
four years for Taurasi with eighteen months in wood; three for Aglianico del Taburno
the Irpinia DOC sub-zone for Aglianico from the Taurasi communes released young
the three sub-zones of Costa d'Amalfi DOC
dove's foot, the Neapolitan name for Piedirosso
Greco di Tufo and Falanghina are both made as sparkling wines within their DOCs
tiers: Taurasi DOCG
At least 85 per cent Aglianico from Taurasi and sixteen other communes; three years of ageing with at least one in wood, the Riserva four years with eighteen months in wood. DOC 1970, DOCG 1993.
Fiano di Avellino DOCG
At least 85 per cent Fiano from twenty-six communes around Avellino, Greco, Coda di Volpe or Trebbiano for the rest; the label may add the Latin Apianum. DOCG 2003.
Greco di Tufo DOCG
At least 85 per cent Greco from eight communes around Tufo with Coda di Volpe for the rest; still or traditional method spumante. DOCG 2003.
Aglianico del Taburno DOCG
At least 85 per cent Aglianico from the Taburno massif near Benevento; two years of ageing, three for the Riserva; also a rosato. DOCG 2011.
Irpinia DOC
The provincial DOC of 2005 for varietal Aglianico, Fiano, Greco, Falanghina and Coda di Volpe outside the DOCG rules, with the Campi Taurasini sub-zone for Aglianico.
Vesuvio DOC
Lacryma Christi del Vesuvio: Rosso led by Piedirosso, Bianco by Coda di Volpe or Caprettone, grown on the volcano's slopes.
Costa d'Amalfi DOC
Whites of Falanghina and Biancolella, reds of Piedirosso and Aglianico from the terraces, with Furore, Ravello and Tramonti as named sub-zones.
Falanghina del Sannio DOC
The Benevento province's varietal Falanghina DOC of 2011, with Solopaca, Guardia Sanframondi, Sant'Agata de' Goti and Taburno as sub-zones.

made.viticulture: Irpinia is high, wet and cold for the south, so the choices are those of a mountain vineyard: south and west facing slopes, Guyot and spur pruned cordon replacing the old raggiera and tendone pergolas, and canopy work to dry the fruit after autumn rain. Aglianico buds early and ripens last, picked in late October or November, sometimes after the first snow on the peaks, and its hard tannin needs the full season; it is prone to spring frost and to rot in a wet harvest. Fiano is thick skinned and resists the damp; Greco is tight bunched and rots easily, so growers pick it at the first sign. Phylloxera and the war emptied Irpinia's vineyards, and one Atripalda house kept the three grapes in cultivation, which is why the region still has them. On Vesuvius and in the Campi Flegrei the volcanic sand kept phylloxera out, and ungrafted vines of Piedirosso and Falanghina survive on their own roots. The Amalfi coast and Ischia farm by hand on dry stone terraces over the sea, the Amalfi vines on chestnut pergolas.
made.winemaking: Taurasi is made as a slow red: long maceration to extract and begin softening Aglianico's tannin, then at least a year in wood, in large Slavonian casks by the traditional houses and in barrique by the modern ones, and the balance of its three years in cellar and bottle; the Riserva takes four years with eighteen months of wood. The whites are made in steel, cool and reductive, with a few months on the lees; some Fiano is fermented or aged in used oak for texture, and the best Greco is held on its lees for months before release. Greco di Tufo is also made as a traditional method sparkling wine within the DOCG. Falanghina is fermented cold and bottled early for freshness, and in the Campi Flegrei makes a sparkling base as well. Lacryma Christi reds are fermented briefly for a light, drinkable wine. On the coast, Costa d'Amalfi's top white is barrel fermented from late picked local grapes.

places.name: Irpinia
places.note: The province of Avellino in the Apennines east of Naples, high, cold and wet, where the three DOCGs lie within a few kilometres of each other on clay, limestone and volcanic ash. The first DOCG of the south and the only southern whites with a reputation for ageing come from here.

places.name: Taurasi
places.note: The village on the Calore above Avellino that gives its name to the Aglianico DOCG of seventeen communes; the hills rise from 300 to 700 metres, Montemarano and Castelfranci the highest and latest.

places.name: Montemarano
places.note: The high, cold southern end of the Taurasi zone, above 600 metres, where Aglianico is picked in November and the wines are the most austere.

places.name: Avellino and the Fiano villages
places.note: Fiano di Avellino's twenty-six communes ring the provincial capital, Lapio, Montefredane and Summonte among the names on single vineyard labels.

places.name: Tufo
places.note: A village on the Sabato north of Avellino named for its volcanic tuff, with old sulphur mines under the vineyards that growers credit for the flinty edge of Greco di Tufo; eight communes make up the DOCG.

places.name: Santa Paolina and Montefusco
places.note: Two of the Greco di Tufo communes on the higher ground above Tufo, the source of the most mineral and long lived examples.

places.name: Sannio and the Taburno
places.note: The province of Benevento north of Irpinia, warmer and lower, with the Taburno massif's Aglianico DOCG and the Falanghina del Sannio DOC; Solopaca, Guardia Sanframondi and Sant'Agata de' Goti are its villages and sub-zones.

places.name: Vesuvius
places.note: The volcano east of Naples, whose ash and lava carry the Vesuvio DOC and the Lacryma Christi wines on ungrafted Piedirosso and Caprettone vines; the ancient vineyards at Pompeii have been replanted inside the ruins.

places.name: Campi Flegrei
places.note: The burning fields west of Naples, a caldera of yellow tuff and volcanic sand where Falanghina and Piedirosso grow on their own roots; the DOC names the two grapes as varietal wines.

places.name: The Amalfi coast, Sorrento and the islands
places.note: Costa d'Amalfi DOC on the terraces of Furore, Ravello and Tramonti; Penisola Sorrentina with the fizzy red of Gragnano; Ischia DOC with Biancolella and Forastera; and tiny Capri DOC. All hand worked and saline.

places.name: Caserta and the Massico
places.note: The northern province: Falerno del Massico DOC on Monte Massico and the edge of the Roccamonfina volcano, heir of Rome's Falernian, with Aglianico and Piedirosso reds and Falanghina whites; the Bourbon vines Pallagrello and Casavecchia; Asprinio di Aversa trained up poplars.

places.name: Salerno and the Cilento
places.note: The south of the region: the Cilento DOC on the coast below Paestum, and the Colli di Salerno IGT, under which Montevetrano's Cabernet, Merlot and Aglianico blend opened the south to the world in the 1990s.

places.name: Basilicata, the neighbour to the east
places.note: The sheet carries no Basilicata locator, so its one great wine sits here: Aglianico del Vulture, from the slopes of the extinct Monte Vulture volcano around Rionero and Barile, a DOC since 1971 with Aglianico del Vulture Superiore a DOCG since 2010 (three years of ageing, Riserva five). The same grape as Taurasi, in a different region and on lava rather than clay. Calabria's Cirò, from Gaglioppo, is the other neighbour's red.

producers.name: Mastroberardino
producers.why: The Atripalda house that kept Aglianico, Fiano and Greco alive through the twentieth century and whose Taurasi vintages of the 1960s proved the wine could age; Radici is its Taurasi and it replanted the vineyards of Pompeii.

producers.name: Feudi di San Gregorio
producers.why: Founded in 1986 at Sorbo Serpico, the modern face of Irpinia: polished Taurasi, Fiano and Greco, the Serpico old vine Aglianico and the Pàtrimo Merlot.

producers.name: Quintodecimo
producers.why: A Mirabella Eclano estate founded by a professor of oenology, making single vineyard Taurasi, Fiano and Greco of great polish.

producers.name: Montevetrano
producers.why: A Colli di Salerno IGT blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Aglianico from the hills above Salerno, first made in 1991, that showed the south could make a world class wine outside the DOC rules.

producers.name: Cuomo (Furore)
producers.why: The Amalfi coast estate at Furore sold under its founder's full name, whose Fiorduva, a barrel fermented white from late picked Fenile, Ginestra and Ripoli on cliff terraces, is the coast's one famous wine.

producers.name: Terredora
producers.why: The Irpinia house born of the 1994 division of the Mastroberardino family's vineyards, with Taurasi, Fiano and Greco from its own sites around Montefusco.

producers.name: Pietracupa
producers.why: A small Montefredane estate whose Fiano and Greco are the growers' benchmarks for tension and longevity in Irpinia.

producers.name: Caggiano
producers.why: A Taurasi village estate whose Vigna Macchia dei Goti Taurasi and Salae Domini Aglianico defined the modern, barrique aged style of the 1990s.

producers.name: Molettieri
producers.why: A Montemarano grower at the high, cold end of Taurasi, whose Cinque Querce Riserva is the austere mountain expression of the DOCG.

producers.name: Villa Matilde
producers.why: The Cellole estate that revived Falerno del Massico in the 1960s from the Roman Falernian and makes Aglianico and Falanghina on the Roccamonfina volcano.

producers.name: Mustilli
producers.why: The Sant'Agata de' Goti house that bottled the first varietal Falanghina in 1979 and gave the Sannio its white.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean on the bay and the coast, warm and dry, with sea breezes along the Amalfi cliffs and the islands. Irpinia is another country: 400 to 700 metres up in the Apennines, with cold winters, snow, heavy rain and a harvest that runs into November for Aglianico, among the latest of any Italian red. The day to night swing in the hills is what holds acidity in Fiano and Greco.
terroir.soils: Volcanic ground is the region's signature: Vesuvius ash and lava on the bay, the yellow tuff of the Campi Flegrei caldera, the Roccamonfina volcano in the north and layers of pumice and ash that the eruptions spread over Irpinia's clay and limestone. Tufo is named for its tuff and once mined for sulphur; Taurasi's hills are clay and limestone with volcanic layers; the Amalfi coast is limestone and dolomite terraces.
terroir.topography: The Apennines run down the inland spine, and the wine hills of Irpinia and the Sannio sit on their western flank between 300 and 700 metres. The bay of Naples is ringed by Vesuvius to the east and the Campi Flegrei to the west; the Sorrento peninsula and the Amalfi coast drop from 1,000 metre mountains to the sea in terraces, and Ischia and Capri rise offshore.
terroir.water: The Tyrrhenian Sea on three gulfs, Gaeta, Naples and Salerno; the Volturno in the north and the Calore and the Sabato in Irpinia, whose valleys hold the Taurasi and Tufo vineyards. Ischia, Procida and Capri are islands; the Campi Flegrei is a caldera.

traps: Taurasi is Aglianico from Campania; Aglianico del Vulture is Basilicata. Same grape, two regions, and the atlas keeps Vulture out of the Campania locator.
Greco di Tufo is not Greco di Bianco: the Calabrian wine is a sweet passito from a different vine.
Fiano di Avellino is the DOCG; Fiano grown elsewhere in Campania or in Puglia is only Fiano.
Lacryma Christi is a style within the Vesuvio DOC, not a grape and not a DOCG.
Falanghina is two distinct varieties, Beneventana and Flegrea, under one name; the exam wants only the name.
Taurasi's Riserva is four years, not five; Brunello's clock is Tuscany's.
Aglianico is pale next to Montepulciano and tannic next to everything; do not read its garnet rim as age.
Coda di Volpe is a grape; Caprettone, the Vesuvius white long sold under that name, is a separate vine.

wines.note: Aglianico aged at least three years, one in wood: dark cherry, smoke, tar, leather and dried herbs over high acid and firm tannin, closed when young and best after ten years. Decant; lamb, braised goat, aged caciocavallo.
The same wine held four years with eighteen months in wood, the extra time softening the grip; the Riserva vintages of the old houses can live forty years.
Dry and medium to full, hazelnut, pear, honeysuckle and smoke, with weight more than cut; a white to serve at cellar temperature with roast chicken, mushroom pasta or buffalo mozzarella.

Taut and mineral, peach and quince with bitter almond and a flinty edge from the sulphur ground; higher in acid than Fiano. Oysters, grilled fish and fried seafood; also made as a traditional method sparkling.
Crisp, citrus and apple, unoaked and meant young: the house white of the region's trattorie, with fried anchovies and pizza.
The tears of Christ: a Piedirosso led red from the ash of Vesuvius, light, peppery and sour cherried; the Bianco is Coda di Volpe or Caprettone. Pasta with tomato and the Neapolitan table.
The Sannio's Aglianico DOCG, often softer and earlier drinking than Taurasi, from the hills around Benevento, with two years of ageing and a Riserva at three.
Falanghina and Biancolella from cliff terraces above the sea at Furore: saline, lemon and herb, with a famous barrel fermented Fiorduva from late picked local grapes. Seafood, lemon pasta.

exam: Lambrusco is a family of grapes and of separate DOCs: Sorbara (pale, sharp, at least 60 per cent Sorbara), Grasparossa di Castelvetro (dark, tannic, foothills) and Salamino di Santa Croce (deep, fruity, plain).
Know the sweetness words on a Lambrusco label: secco, amabile and dolce.
Most Lambrusco is made by the tank (Charmat) method, frizzante or spumante; bottle refermentation, the traditional method and the ancestral method also appear.
Romagna Albana was raised in 1987 as the first white DOCG in Italy; it is dry or sweet, the passito from dried grapes.
Romagna's red is Sangiovese, sold as Romagna Sangiovese with Superiore, Riserva and subzone names.
Place the region: it straddles north and central Italy, with the Po to the north, the Apennines to the south and the Adriatic to the east; the Court files it as cool continental.
Serve Lambrusco cold in a flute or a white wine glass with Parmigiano Reggiano, salumi and dishes dressed with balsamic vinegar; an opened bottle loses its sparkle quickly, so watch it by the glass.

grapes.name: Lambrusco di Sorbara
grapes.styles: The pale member of the family: it sets fruit poorly and gives thin bunches, so its wine is light ruby to deep pink, sharply acidic and scented with violets and sour cherry.

grapes.name: Lambrusco Grasparossa
grapes.styles: Named for its stalks, which turn red at harvest; grown in the foothills around Castelvetro, it gives dark, full and tannic Lambrusco, the opposite pole to Sorbara.

grapes.name: Lambrusco Salamino
grapes.styles: Named for its small, cylindrical bunches shaped like a salami; planted widely on the plain around Carpi and Reggio, it gives deep colour and round, fruity wine.

grapes.name: Ancellotta
grapes.styles: A deeply coloured red blended into Lambrusco, above all in Reggio Emilia, for colour and softness.

grapes.name: Sangiovese
grapes.styles: Romagna's red, grown on the hills from Imola to Rimini: sour cherry, violet and firm acid, light in plain Romagna Sangiovese and more structured in the Superiore, the Riserva and the subzone wines.

grapes.name: Albana
grapes.styles: Romagna's native white, thick skinned, with high acid and a little tannin for a white: dry wines with a bitter almond finish, and sweet passito from dried or botrytised grapes.

grapes.name: Trebbiano Romagnolo
grapes.styles: The workhorse white of the Romagna plain, neutral and productive, sold as Romagna Trebbiano and in IGT blends.

grapes.name: Pignoletto
grapes.styles: Grechetto Gentile by its variety name, grown in the Bologna hills for crisp still and frizzante whites with apple, herbs and a light bitter finish.

grapes.name: Malvasia di Candia Aromatica
grapes.styles: The aromatic white of the Piacenza and Parma hills, made dry, frizzante or passito, scented with orange blossom and peach.

grapes.name: Barbera
grapes.styles: With Croatina the base of Gutturnio, the red of the Piacenza hills, where it brings acid and bright fruit.

grapes.name: Croatina
grapes.styles: Called Bonarda in the Piacenza hills, it gives Gutturnio its colour, dark fruit and tannin.

law.classification: Italian law sets the ladder: DOCG, DOC and IGT, the Italian name for an IGP. In 2026 Emilia-Romagna holds two DOCGs: Romagna Albana, raised in 1987 as Albana di Romagna, the first white DOCG in Italy, and Colli Bolognesi Pignoletto in the Bologna hills, raised in 2010. There is no single Lambrusco DOC. The Court lists Sorbara, Grasparossa di Castelvetro and Salamino di Santa Croce as subzones, but each is a DOC of its own, all three recognised in 1970, beside the broader Reggiano and Modena DOCs. A great deal of Lambrusco is sold as IGT Emilia, also written dell'Emilia. The Romagna DOC covers Sangiovese, Trebbiano and sparkling wines and lets a Sangiovese name one of its subzones. In the west, the Colli Piacentini DOC and the Gutturnio DOC, separated from it in 2010, hold the Piacenza hills.
labels: refermented in its own bottle, usually unfiltered, with a sediment
tiers: Romagna Albana DOCG
Albana from the Romagna hills, secco, amabile, dolce or passito; raised in 1987 as Albana di Romagna, the first white DOCG in Italy.
Colli Bolognesi Pignoletto DOCG
Whites of Grechetto Gentile from the hills south-west of Bologna, DOCG since 2010; its Classico wine takes at least 95 per cent Grechetto Gentile.
Lambrusco di Sorbara DOC
At least 60 per cent Sorbara, the rest mainly Salamino; frizzante or spumante, secco to dolce.
Lambrusco Grasparossa di Castelvetro DOC
At least 85 per cent Grasparossa, from the plain and foothills south of Modena.
Lambrusco Salamino di Santa Croce DOC
Salamino led, from the plain around Carpi, north of Modena.
Reggiano DOC and Modena DOC
The broader Lambrusco DOCs of the two provinces, blends of several Lambrusco varieties, often softened with Ancellotta in Reggio.
Romagna DOC
Sangiovese, Trebbiano and sparkling wines across Romagna; Romagna Sangiovese may add Superiore, Riserva and a subzone name.
Gutturnio DOC
Barbera 55 to 70 per cent with Croatina 30 to 45 per cent from the Piacenza hills; a DOC of its own since 2010.
Emilia IGT
The regional IGT, also labelled dell'Emilia, the source of much Lambrusco sold under the family name.

made.viticulture: On the plain, vines were long trained up trees in the old mixed farms, and today high, vigorous trellises such as the Sylvoz and the double curtain carry generous crops of Lambrusco and Trebbiano for the frizzante and bulk trade. The hill vineyards are trained lower, on spurred cordon or Guyot, and give smaller, riper crops. Lambrusco di Sorbara sets fruit poorly, which is why its DOC lets Salamino make up to 40 per cent of the wine. Albana's thick skins resist rot, so it can hang into the foggy autumn for passito or for noble rot. The hazards are fungal disease on the humid plain, spring frost in the hollows, summer hail and, more often now, drought in hot summers.
made.winemaking: Most Lambrusco is made in two steps: a dry base wine, then a second fermentation in a pressure tank, the Charmat or Martinotti method, stopped by chilling and filtering when the sparkle and the sweetness are right. Frizzante wines carry a light sparkle of about 1 to 2.5 bar, spumante a full one. The older way, refermentation in the bottle, leaves a cloudy sediment and has come back with small growers, and a few make Lambrusco by the traditional method or the ancestral method. Skin contact is short, so even dark Lambrusco is light in tannin, and Sorbara can be pressed almost as a rosé. Romagna's Sangiovese is fermented in steel or wood and aged in cask for Riserva; Albana passito comes from bunches dried on racks or picked late with noble rot; and the Piacenza hills keep a habit of skin fermented whites from Malvasia di Candia.

places.name: Modena
places.note: The Lambrusco heart of Emilia, the plain and foothills around the city of balsamic vinegar, holding the three DOCs the Court names.

places.name: Sorbara
places.note: A village on the plain north of Modena between the Secchia and the Panaro, whose sandy alluvium grows the pale, sharp Lambrusco di Sorbara.

places.name: Castelvetro
places.note: A hill town south of Modena at the heart of Lambrusco Grasparossa di Castelvetro, on clay and marl foothills that give a dark, tannic wine.

places.name: Santa Croce
places.note: A village near Carpi, north of Modena, that names Lambrusco Salamino di Santa Croce, the deep, fruity Lambrusco of the plain.

places.name: Reggio Emilia
places.note: The province west of Modena, home of the Reggiano DOC, whose Lambrusco blends often take Ancellotta and come off dry or sweet, and of the large cooperatives behind the export trade.

places.name: Colli di Scandiano e di Canossa
places.note: The hills south of Reggio, a DOC for Lambrusco and for sparkling whites from the local Spergola.

places.name: Colli Piacentini
places.note: The hills south of Piacenza on the Lombard border, a DOC for the white Ortrugo, aromatic Malvasia di Candia and the rare sweet Vin Santo di Vigoleno.

places.name: Gutturnio
places.note: The red of the Piacenza hills, Barbera with Croatina, still or frizzante, with Superiore and Riserva wines; a DOC of its own since 2010.

places.name: Colli di Parma
places.note: The hills south of Parma, the prosciutto country, for frizzante Malvasia and light reds of Barbera and Croatina.

places.name: Colli Bolognesi
places.note: The hills south-west of Bologna, home of the Colli Bolognesi Pignoletto DOCG for Grechetto Gentile whites, still or frizzante. The DOCG was created in 2010 as Colli Bolognesi Classico Pignoletto and renamed in 2014, when a broader Pignoletto DOC was drawn around it; that DOC has been named Emilia-Romagna DOC since the 2024 harvest.

places.name: Romagna
places.note: The eastern half, from Imola to Rimini, where hills of clay, marl and spungone run down towards the Adriatic: Sangiovese for red, Albana and Trebbiano for white.

places.name: The Romagna Sangiovese subzones
places.note: Romagna Sangiovese may name a hill subzone on its label, among them Bertinoro, Brisighella, Modigliana, Predappio, Oriolo and Serra: spungone at Bertinoro and Brisighella, sandstone and marl high in the Apennines at Modigliana.

places.name: Bosco Eliceo
places.note: Sandy coastal land by the Po delta between Ferrara and Ravenna, where Fortana makes a light, sharp and often frizzante red.

producers.name: Cleto Chiarli
producers.why: A Modena house founded in 1860 and a reference for dry Sorbara and Grasparossa, made both in tank and refermented in bottle.

producers.name: Cavicchioli
producers.why: A house of San Prospero in the Sorbara zone, whose Vigna del Cristo is a single vineyard Lambrusco di Sorbara.

producers.name: Paltrinieri
producers.why: A Sorbara family estate whose pale, dry Lambrusco di Sorbara, bottle refermented wines among them, shows the grape's sharp, pale edge.

producers.name: Medici Ermete
producers.why: A Reggio Emilia house whose dry Concerto helped restore the name of dry Reggiano Lambrusco.

producers.name: Cantine Riunite
producers.why: The Reggio Emilia cooperative whose sweet, lightly sparkling Lambrusco became a large seller in the United States from the 1970s.

producers.name: Fattoria Zerbina
producers.why: A Faenza estate whose Scacco Matto, a botrytised Albana passito, makes the case for Albana's DOCG, beside serious Romagna Sangiovese.

producers.name: La Stoppa
producers.why: A historic estate of the Colli Piacentini known for long aged Barbera and Bonarda reds and for Ageno, a skin fermented white led by Malvasia di Candia.

terroir.climate: The Court files the region as cool continental, and the Po plain fits it: cold, foggy winters, hot and humid summers and rain in spring and autumn. The Apennine foothills are a little cooler and better aired than the plain, and Romagna, open to the Adriatic, is milder and sunnier, with sea breezes reaching its hills. Fog and humidity bring rot and mildew; hail and spring frost are the other hazards.
terroir.soils: The plain is deep alluvium laid down by the Po and its Apennine tributaries: fertile silt, clay and sand. Sorbara's vineyards lie on lighter, sandier alluvium between the Secchia and the Panaro, while Grasparossa grows on the clay and marl of the foothills south of Modena. Romagna's hills are clay, marl and sandstone, crossed by a band of yellow, fossil-rich calcarenite the growers call spungone and by a ridge of gypsum near Brisighella.
terroir.topography: A long, flat plain falls gently from the mountains to the Po, cut by the Roman road, the Via Emilia, that strings the cities together: Piacenza, Parma, Reggio, Modena, Bologna, and in Romagna Imola, Faenza, Forlì, Cesena and Rimini. South of the road a band of low hills, the colli, rises towards the Apennine ridge, and that is where the finer vineyards sit: the Colli Piacentini, the Colli di Parma, the Colli Bolognesi and the Romagna hills.
terroir.water: The Po forms most of the northern border, and its tributaries, the Trebbia, Taro, Secchia, Panaro and Reno among them, run north out of the mountains across the plain. Their silt makes the plain fertile and their valleys draw cool air down from the hills. The Adriatic tempers eastern Romagna, and the sandy ground of the Po delta near Ferrara grows the Fortana of Bosco Eliceo.

traps: There is no single Lambrusco DOC: the Court's subzones are separate DOCs, and much Lambrusco is IGT Emilia.
Dry Lambrusco is the local tradition; the sweet export style is one choice, not the definition.
Lambrusco Mantovano is made in the province of Mantua, in Lombardy, not in Emilia-Romagna.
Albana was the first white DOCG, not the first DOCG: red DOCGs such as Brunello di Montalcino and Barolo came before it.
Pignoletto is Grechetto Gentile, the Grechetto di Todi of Umbria, not the Grechetto of Orvieto.
Gutturnio is a wine, not a grape: a blend of Barbera and Croatina, which the Piacenza hills call Bonarda.
Romagna Sangiovese is a wine of the Adriatic side of the Apennines, not a Tuscan wine, though the grape is shared.

wines.note: Pale ruby to deep pink, frothy and dry in its classic form, with violets, wild strawberry and sharp acidity. Serve it cold beside prosciutto, mortadella and gnocco fritto.
Deep purple with a violet foam, blackberry and plum and a dry, firm grip of tannin; the Lambrusco for zampone, cotechino and the rich pork dishes of Modena.
Deep ruby, fruity and round, dry or off dry; an all round partner for salumi and Parmigiano Reggiano.
Soft, grapey and medium sweet, often coloured with Ancellotta: the style of Reggio's large cooperatives that carried Lambrusco to American tables from the 1970s. Serve it well chilled.
Medium bodied, with sour cherry, violet and an earthy, savoury edge; the Superiore and Riserva wines of the hills carry more weight. Pour it with ragù, roast meats and piadina with cured ham.
Golden, full and faintly tannic, with apricot, almond and a bitter twist; serve it with fish stews, white meats and fresh cheeses.
From dried, often botrytised grapes: honey, apricot and saffron over fresh acidity, with blue cheese or almond pastries.
Barbera and Croatina from the Piacenza hills, still or frizzante: dark cherry, fresh acid and soft tannin, with coppa and the other salumi of Piacenza.

grapes.name: Friulano
grapes.styles: The native white, Sauvignonasse by DNA and Tocai Friulano until the name was lost in 2007: pear, almond, a bitter-nut finish, medium acid; the region's own glass with prosciutto di San Daniele.

grapes.name: Ribolla Gialla
grapes.styles: A high-acid, lemon-and-flower white of Collio and Oslavia, grown as Rebula across the border; the grape of the orange wine movement and of Friuli's sparkling boom.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Friuli's commercial engine, better than the plain average when from Collio or Isonzo: pear, nectarine, weight; also made as a coppery ramato with brief skin contact.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Grassy, flinty and ripe from the hills; the Collio's most sought-after international white.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: Pinot Bianco: creamy and discreet, the quiet partner in Collio Bianco blends and a fine varietal in Isonzo.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Widely planted, often part of the great white blends.

grapes.name: Malvasia Istriana
grapes.styles: An aromatic, salty Malvasia of Carso and Collio, apricot and herbs.

grapes.name: Verduzzo
grapes.styles: A tannic white making dry wine and the sweet Ramandolo on the foothills.

grapes.name: Picolit
grapes.styles: A sweet white of tiny yields, the eighteenth-century dessert wine of European courts; Colli Orientali del Friuli Picolit DOCG.

grapes.name: Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso
grapes.styles: The native red with the red stem: dark, plummy, high acid, a bitter edge; the everyday red of plain and hills.

grapes.name: Schioppettino
grapes.styles: Prepotto's peppery, violet-scented red, revived from a few vines in the 1970s; also called Ribolla Nera.

grapes.name: Pignolo
grapes.styles: A rare, intensely tannic red of Rosazzo revived for long ageing.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: The most planted red of the region, soft and fruity on the plain.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: Much of Friuli's Cabernet Franc proved to be Carmenère; leafy, red-fruited and light.

grapes.name: Vitovska
grapes.styles: Carso's white, lean and saline, often skin fermented.

grapes.name: Terrano
grapes.styles: Carso's red, a Refosco relative, sharp and iron-rich.

grapes.name: Glera
grapes.styles: The village of Prosecco sits above Trieste, which is why the Prosecco DOC takes in all of Friuli.

law.classification: The hills carry two senior DOCs, Collio (or Collio Goriziano, 1968) in the province of Gorizia and Friuli Colli Orientali (1970) in the province of Udine, both named for their marl hills and both varietal-led: the grape name follows the zone name on the label. The plain is covered by Friuli Grave (the largest), Friuli Isonzo, Friuli Aquileia, Friuli Latisana and Friuli Annia, with Carso above Trieste and Lison-Pramaggiore shared with Veneto. Friuli DOC, created in 2016, blankets the whole region for varietal wines and sparkling Ribolla Gialla. Four DOCGs are all small: Ramandolo (2001, sweet Verduzzo), Colli Orientali del Friuli Picolit (2006), Rosazzo (2011, a Friulano-led white blend) and Lison (Tai, shared with Veneto). Delle Venezie DOC (2017) takes the plain's Pinot Grigio across three regions, and the Prosecco DOC reaches the whole region.

made.viticulture: Vines on the hills are Guyot trained on ponca terraces that crumble and need constant rebuilding; on the gravel plain rows are longer and often machine harvested. Whites are picked early for acid in a wet climate, and the growers' chief enemy is rot, so canopies are opened, bunches thinned and sprays timed to the rain. Picolit's flowers abort, so a bunch carries a handful of berries and the yield per vine is tiny, which is why the wine is rare and dear. Verduzzo for Ramandolo is picked late and partly dried. Schioppettino, Pignolo and Tazzelenghe were nearly lost after phylloxera and the wars and were replanted from relic vines from the 1970s. The Carso's vines grow in pockets of red earth among the limestone, braced against the Bora; Vitovska and Terrano are its own.
made.winemaking: The modern Friulian white took shape in the 1960s: cold, slow fermentation in stainless steel under protection from oxygen, clean yeast, little or no malolactic, early bottling, varietal purity on the label. That became the template for Italian white wine. The region then went two further ways. The hills' top blends (Collio Bianco and the famous estate cuvées) took barrel fermentation and lees ageing for texture. And Oslavia, a hamlet of Collio above Gorizia, turned back towards the oldest method: Ribolla Gialla and Pinot Grigio fermented on their skins for weeks or months, in open wood or in Georgian clay amphorae buried in the ground, no additions, no temperature control, long ageing, and bottled amber and tannic. That is orange wine, and these are the wines the name was coined for. Sweet wines are late harvest or partly dried (Picolit, Ramandolo, Verduzzo). Ribolla sparkling is tank method; Pinot Grigio ramato takes a few hours of skin contact for a copper tint.

places.name: Collio
places.note: The arc of hills around Cormòns and Gorizia along the Slovenian border, continued as Brda on the other side. Ponca soils, Guyot training, and some of the finest Friulano, Ribolla Gialla, Sauvignon, Pinot Bianco and Pinot Grigio in Italy, plus the Collio Bianco blends; DOC since 1968.

places.name: Oslavia
places.note: The hamlet above Gorizia where Ribolla Gialla on the skins became orange wine from the late 1990s, with amphorae from Georgia; the Gravner and Radikon hill.

places.name: Cormòns
places.note: The market town at the centre of Collio; Capriva, Dolegna and San Floriano around it hold the great estates.

places.name: Friuli Colli Orientali
places.note: The hills of the province of Udine from Cividale north to Tarcento, on the same ponca, cooler and more varied, with the region's native reds and sweet wines. DOC since 1970 as Colli Orientali del Friuli, renamed in 2011.

places.name: Rosazzo
places.note: An abbey hill south of Cividale: Rosazzo DOCG (a Friulano-led white blend) and the Pignolo and Ribolla subzones.

places.name: Prepotto
places.note: Schioppettino's home valley on the border; Schioppettino di Prepotto is a named subzone.

places.name: Cialla
places.note: A side valley with its own subzone for Picolit, Verduzzo and Schioppettino; a single estate revived it from 1970.

places.name: Ramandolo
places.note: On the foothills above Nimis and Tarcento: sweet Verduzzo, DOCG since 2001, Friuli's first.

places.name: Buttrio
places.note: A commune south of Udine with small, high-priced estates on ponca.

places.name: Friuli Isonzo
places.note: The gravel terraces of the Isonzo river south of Gorizia, warmer than Collio and ripening fuller whites; Rive Alte and Rive di Giare are its subzones.

places.name: Friuli Grave
places.note: The gravel plain on both sides of the Tagliamento, reaching west to the Livenza, the largest share of the region's wine: Pinot Grigio, Merlot, Refosco, Friulano, clean and inexpensive.

places.name: Carso
places.note: The limestone karst plateau above Trieste, red earth in pockets of rock, the Bora wind: Vitovska and Malvasia whites, Terrano red, much of it skin fermented; the village of Prosecco lies on its edge.

places.name: The lagoon plain
places.note: Friuli Aquileia, Friuli Latisana and Friuli Annia, the DOCs of the flat land towards the lagoons: light reds and whites for early drinking.

places.name: Lison-Pramaggiore
places.note: The plain shared with Veneto along the Livenza: Lison DOCG for Tai, and Merlot and Refosco under DOC.

producers.name: Jermann

producers.name: Livio Felluga

producers.name: Schiopetto

producers.name: Gravner

producers.name: Radikon
producers.why: Oslavia's other pioneer of skin-fermented Ribolla: long macerations, no added sulphur, its own bottle sizes.

producers.name: Miani

producers.name: Vie di Romans

producers.name: Borgo del Tiglio
producers.why: Cormòns estate of barrel-fermented Friulano and the Collio Bianco Studio di Bianco.

producers.name: Ronchi di Cialla

terroir.climate: Cool to moderate and wet: the Alps shelter the region from the north but the Adriatic sends humidity and rain, and Friuli is among Italy's rainiest wine regions. The hills see large day-night swings that keep aroma and acid; the Carso plateau above Trieste is scoured by the Bora, a cold, dry north-easterly. Hail and harvest rain are the hazards.
terroir.soils: Ponca, the local name for flysch, alternating layers of marl and sandstone laid down under an Eocene sea, defines Collio and the Colli Orientali: it crumbles, drains and holds water at depth. The Grave and Isonzo plains are deep alluvial gravel dropped by the Tagliamento, Meduna and Isonzo rivers, warm by day and quick to drain. Carso is red, iron-rich clay in pockets of limestone karst.
terroir.topography: A crescent of low hills from Cividale through Cormòns to Gorizia along the Slovenian border, rarely above 300 metres, where the best whites grow; a broad flat plain south and west of them to the sea; the Carso limestone plateau above Trieste; and the pre-Alps behind, where Ramandolo sits on the foothills near Nimis.
terroir.water: The Tagliamento and Isonzo rivers built the gravel plains and name the Grave and Isonzo zones; the lagoons of Grado and Marano and the Gulf of Trieste bring sea air to the south. The Bora off the karst keeps the Carso dry.

traps: Friulano is not Furmint and has nothing to do with Tokaj; it is Sauvignonasse, the Sauvignon Vert of Chile.
Collio is in Gorizia province, the Colli Orientali in Udine; both are DOC, not DOCG. Rosazzo inside the Colli Orientali is the DOCG.
Orange wine is white grapes on their skins, not a rosé and not oxidised by definition; the colour comes from skin tannin and time.
Grave in Friuli means gravel, like Graves in Bordeaux; it is the plain, not a quality tier.
Ribolla Gialla is Rebula in Slovenia; Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso is named for its red stem, not for a red variety of Refosco.
The village of Prosecco is in Friuli, so Prosecco DOC covers Friuli; the Prosecco DOCGs are in Veneto.
Ramandolo is the DOCG for sweet Verduzzo, not for Picolit; Picolit's DOCG carries the Colli Orientali name.
Picolit's tiny crop comes from floral abortion, not from botrytis or drying alone.

wines.note: Dry, medium weight, pear, white peach and a bitter almond close; the local aperitivo with prosciutto and frico.
The hills' blended white, Friulano, Ribolla, Pinot Bianco, Sauvignon and more, often the estate's top cuvée and sometimes oaked.
Lemon, white flowers, lively acid and little body when fresh from steel; sparkling by the tank method across the plain; amber, tannic and savoury when skin fermented in Oslavia.
Ripe pear and a touch of spice from the hills; the plain makes the Delle Venezie volume.
Elderflower, grapefruit, nettle and flint; dry, taut, a match for asparagus and goat's cheese.
Weeks to months on the skins, often in amphora or old wood, sometimes unfined: amber, dried apricot, tea tannin, nutty; serve cool, not cold, with rich or spiced food.
Dark plum, violet, black pepper, high acid, a bitter cherry finish; drinks young and suits goulash and game.
Pepper and violets over red fruit, mid-weight and elegant, the Colli Orientali's most prized native red.
Golden, honeyed, apricot and acacia, a meditation wine poured in small glasses with dry pastries.
Verduzzo picked late and partly dried on the foothills near Nimis: amber, tannic, sweet, for cheese.
Friuli's share of the Prosecco DOC; Trieste may appear on the label as a subzone.

grapes.name: Nero d'Avola

grapes.name: Glera

grapes.name: Garganega

grapes.name: Vermentino

grapes.name: Nerello Mascalese

grapes.name: Cortese

grapes.name: Dolcetto

grapes.name: Lambrusco

grapes.name: Chardonnay

grapes.name: Merlot

The top: a DOC of at least seven years' standing, tighter yields and ageing, panel tasting, and the numbered state seal (fascetta) on the neck. The first four were granted in 1980

italy.overview:
The Greeks called the south Oenotria, the land of trained vines, and the Romans carried the vine north to the Alps; the shape of Italian wine has not changed much since. Vines grow everywhere because the peninsula is a spine of hills, the Apennines, between two seas, with the Alps across the top and two large islands below. Altitude and the sea are the two levers: the north is continental and alpine, the centre is hill country, the south and the islands are Mediterranean and plant high to escape the heat.

The law came late. The first DOC rules date from 1963, the first DOCs were granted in 1966 (Vernaccia di San Gimignano was the first), and the first DOCGs in 1980 went to Brunello di Montalcino, Barolo, Barbaresco and Vino Nobile di Montepulciano. In 1992 the Goria law added IGT, the broad geographic tier that gave a legal home to the Super Tuscans, which had been selling as table wine for twenty years. The EU reform that took effect in 2009 folded DOCG and DOC into DOP and IGT into IGP, and Italy kept its own words on the label. Under the current code an IGT must stand for five years before it can become a DOC, and a DOC for seven before DOCG.

Read a DOCG as a promise of control, not of quality: a numbered state strip across the capsule (the fascetta), tasting by panel, tighter yields and longer ageing. Some of the country's most expensive wines are IGT by choice. Learn each appellation's own meaning for Riserva and Superiore, because the minimums differ from one to the next, and read Classico as the historic heart of a zone rather than a rank.

The exam divides Italy north and south. North means Nebbiolo in Piedmont, the traditional method in Franciacorta and Trento, tank Prosecco, Soave and the Valpolicella family in Veneto, and alpine whites in Alto Adige and Friuli. Centre and south means Sangiovese in Tuscany and its three great DOCGs, the Montepulciano name trap, Aglianico in Campania and Basilicata, Primitivo and Negroamaro in Puglia, Etna and Marsala in Sicily, Cannonau and Vermentino in Sardinia. Hold the grape behind every place name and the method behind every style, and the rest is geography.

traps: DOCG is a control level, not a quality rank; a Toscana IGT can outprice every DOCG on the list.
Montepulciano is a Tuscan town (Vino Nobile, Sangiovese) and an Abruzzese grape (Montepulciano d'Abruzzo); never the same wine.
Riserva has no national minimum; each disciplinare sets it, from a year to five.
Classico is the old heart of a zone, not a higher tier; Chianti Classico is a separate DOCG from Chianti.
Prosecco, Asti and Lambrusco are tank method; Franciacorta, Trento and Alta Langa are bottle fermented.
Amarone is dry, Recioto sweet, Ripasso neither; Sforzato is Valtellina's dried-grape dry Nebbiolo.
Trebbiano Abruzzese and Trebbiano di Soave are not Trebbiano Toscano, though the wine Trebbiano d'Abruzzo may be made from Abruzzese or Toscano; Bonarda means three different grapes in three places.
Vino da Tavola is gone; the base tier is simply Vino, and a Vino Varietale may name its grape.

exam: Lazio is the region of Rome: the Tyrrhenian Sea to the west, the Apennines to the east; maritime on the coast, continental inland.
Frascati: the Malvasia led white of the volcanic Castelli Romani, a DOC since 1966, with Frascati Superiore and Cannellino di Frascati DOCGs since 2011.
Know the three DOCGs as of 2026: Cesanese del Piglio (red, 2008), Frascati Superiore and Cannellino di Frascati (both white, 2011).
Cesanese is Lazio's native red, from Cesanese di Affile and Cesanese Comune; Piglio lies in the province of Frosinone.
Est! Est!! Est!!! di Montefiascone is the Procanico led white of Lake Bolsena, with its legend of the bishop's servant.
Volcanic soils run through the region: Bolsena, Vico, Bracciano and the Alban Hills.
Superiore means riper wine with a higher minimum alcohol; Riserva means longer ageing.

grapes.name: Malvasia del Lazio
grapes.styles: Also called Malvasia Puntinata for the dots on its berries: the scented quality white of Frascati and the Castelli Romani, with peach, apricot and a soft, full texture.

grapes.name: Malvasia Bianca di Candia
grapes.styles: The more widely planted Malvasia of the region, productive and less aromatic, the bulk of many Frascati blends beside Malvasia del Lazio.

grapes.name: Trebbiano Toscano
grapes.styles: Called Procanico around Montefiascone, where it leads Est! Est!! Est!!!; elsewhere it adds neutral freshness to Malvasia.

grapes.name: Bellone
grapes.styles: An old local white revived on the coast around Anzio and Nettuno and in the Castelli Romani: citrus, herbs and a saline finish.

grapes.name: Cesanese
grapes.styles: Lazio's native red, from two vines, the small berried Cesanese di Affile and Cesanese Comune: medium bodied, perfumed with cherry, violet and pepper, with a faint bitter finish.

grapes.name: Montepulciano
grapes.styles: The base of the Roma DOC's red, at least half its blend, beside Cesanese and international grapes.

grapes.name: Aleatico
grapes.styles: A scented red relation of Muscat, made into sweet red wine at Gradoli on Lake Bolsena.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Widely planted for the Lazio IGT reds, from the hills of Montefiascone to the coastal plain south of Rome.

law.classification: In 2026 Lazio holds three DOCGs, a long list of DOCs, many of them small, and the regional Lazio IGT. Cesanese del Piglio, raised in 2008, is the red DOCG. Frascati Superiore and Cannellino di Frascati, both raised in 2011, were carved from the Frascati DOC of 1966, one of Italy's early DOCs, and take at least 70 per cent Malvasia, Bianca di Candia or del Lazio. Est! Est!! Est!!! di Montefiascone, also a DOC of 1966, is led by Trebbiano Toscano. The Roma DOC, created in 2011, covers the province of Rome, its red at least half Montepulciano, its white led by Malvasia del Lazio. Other DOCs include Castelli Romani, Marino, Cesanese di Olevano Romano, Cesanese di Affile, Aleatico di Gradoli and the Lazio side of Orvieto. Superiore marks a riper wine with higher minimum alcohol, Riserva longer ageing.

made.viticulture: The Castelli Romani supplied Rome with wine for centuries, and the bulk trade of the twentieth century brought high trellises and large crops that thinned Frascati's name. Growers seeking quality have since lowered yields, planted more Malvasia del Lazio and returned to the better slopes. Volcanic soils drain fast and hold warmth, so summer drought is a growing hazard, with hail and the humidity that brings mildew. Cesanese ripens late in the cooler hills of the Piglio and is picked in October. On the Agro Pontino, the coastal plain south of Rome reclaimed from marsh in the 1930s, vineyards are flat, trellised and productive.
made.winemaking: Frascati is fermented cool in stainless steel and bottled young; the better producers give Malvasia del Lazio a short skin contact or months on its fine lees for texture, and Frascati Superiore may age as a Riserva. Cannellino di Frascati comes from grapes left on the vine to concentrate, sometimes touched by noble rot, and its fermentation stops with sugar left in the wine. Cesanese is fermented with moderate extraction to keep its perfume and aged in large casks or barrique for the Superiore and Riserva wines. Est! Est!! Est!!! is a cool fermented white, dry or off dry. Aleatico di Gradoli is made sweet, and as a liquoroso fortified with spirit. Across the region, the Lazio IGT covers international grapes from Merlot to Petit Verdot, made in a modern style.

places.name: Castelli Romani
places.note: The ring of hill towns on the rim of the old Alban volcano, around Lakes Albano and Nemi just south-east of Rome, on light, porous volcanic soil: Rome's own vineyard for centuries, with a regional Castelli Romani DOC beside the town DOCs.

places.name: Frascati
places.note: The town that names the Castelli's white, a DOC since 1966; Frascati Superiore and Cannellino di Frascati became DOCGs in 2011, the Cannellino zone taking in Frascati, Grottaferrata, Monte Porzio Catone and parts of Monte Compatri and Rome.

places.name: Marino
places.note: A Castelli town above Lake Albano with a DOC of its own for Malvasia led whites.

places.name: Montefiascone and Lake Bolsena
places.note: A hill town on the rim of the Bolsena crater in the north, home of Est! Est!! Est!!! di Montefiascone, a Procanico led white named for a tale of a bishop's servant who marked the inns where the wine was good.

places.name: Gradoli
places.note: A village above the north-western shore of Lake Bolsena whose DOC makes sweet red Aleatico, still or fortified.

places.name: Piglio
places.note: Hills in the province of Frosinone, south-east of Rome below the Ernici mountains, where Cesanese del Piglio, the red DOCG of 2008, grows on volcanic soil, red clay and limestone.

places.name: Olevano Romano and Affile
places.note: Hill towns north-west of Piglio with Cesanese DOCs of their own; Affile gives its name to the small berried Cesanese di Affile vine.

places.name: Roma
places.note: The Roma DOC of 2011 covers the province of Rome, for Montepulciano led reds and rosés and whites led by Malvasia del Lazio.

places.name: Orvieto in Lazio
places.note: The Orvieto DOC crosses from Umbria into the province of Viterbo; its Lazio side grows the same Grechetto and Procanico whites, taught under Umbria.

places.name: Agro Pontino
places.note: The coastal plain south of Rome around Latina, reclaimed from marsh in the 1930s, a source of international reds and of revived Bellone near Anzio and Nettuno.

producers.name: Fontana Candida
producers.why: A Frascati house whose wines carried Frascati to export markets, with the single vineyard Santa Teresa as its reference Frascati Superiore.

producers.name: Castel de Paolis
producers.why: A Grottaferrata estate that led the revival of quality Frascati from the 1980s, with whites built on Malvasia del Lazio.

producers.name: Principe Pallavicini
producers.why: A noble estate of the Castelli Romani known for Frascati and for varietal Malvasia Puntinata under the Roma DOC.

producers.name: Casale della Ioria
producers.why: A family estate at Acuto in the Piglio zone known for Cesanese del Piglio.

producers.name: Falesco
producers.why: A Montefiascone estate known for Est! Est!! Est!!! and for Montiano, a Merlot sold as IGT.

producers.name: Casale del Giglio
producers.why: An estate on the reclaimed Agro Pontino known for trials of international grapes such as Petit Verdot and for reviving Bellone.
