terroir.climate: Mediterranean on the coast: hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters, with breezes off the Tyrrhenian Sea. The Court files central Italy as maritime on the coast and continental inland, and Lazio's inland hills under the Apennines, around Piglio and Olevano Romano, have colder winters and cooler nights than Rome's plain. The crater lakes temper the hills around them, and drought in hot summers is the growing hazard.
terroir.soils: Volcanic above all. Four main volcanic districts, the Vulsini around Lake Bolsena, the Cimini around Lake Vico, the Sabatini around Lake Bracciano and the Alban Hills south-east of Rome, left ash, tuff and lava that weather into light, porous soils rich in potassium. Inland, the Piglio hills mix volcanic material with red clay and limestone, and the coastal plains south of Rome are sand and reclaimed marsh.
terroir.topography: A coastal plain along the Tyrrhenian, the Roman Campagna, rises inland to volcanic hills ringed with crater lakes and then to the limestone ridges of the Apennines. The Castelli Romani are the hill towns on the rim of the old Alban volcano, looking down on Rome from the south-east. The north, called Tuscia, is a tuff plateau around Lake Bolsena; the south-east, the Ciociaria around Frosinone, is a land of hills below the Ernici mountains.
terroir.water: The Tiber crosses the region to the sea near Ostia. The crater lakes, Bolsena, Vico, Bracciano, Albano and Nemi, soften the extremes on their shores, and the Tyrrhenian moderates the coast and the reclaimed plain of the Agro Pontino.

traps: Cannellino di Frascati is sweet; Frascati and Frascati Superiore are dry.
Cesanese del Piglio is the DOCG; Cesanese di Olevano Romano and Cesanese di Affile are DOCs.
Est! Est!! Est!!! is a white wine and a DOC, not a DOCG.
Malvasia del Lazio (Malvasia Puntinata) and Malvasia Bianca di Candia are two different vines; the first is the scented quality one.
The Orvieto DOC crosses into Lazio, but Orvieto is taught as Umbria's wine.
Montepulciano in a Roma red is the grape, not the Tuscan town of Vino Nobile.
Aleatico di Gradoli is Lazio's sweet red on Lake Bolsena; the Aleatico DOCG of Elba belongs to Tuscany.

wines.note: Dry, light and fresh, with pear, almond and a touch of Malvasia's peach: the everyday white of Rome's trattorie, with fried artichokes, saltimbocca and cacio e pepe.
Riper and fuller, with more of the Malvasia's apricot and a longer, savoury finish; with porchetta, white meats and fish baked in salt.
Golden and sweet from late picked grapes, with honey, apricot and almond; with the ciambelline and dry pastries of the Castelli.
Medium bodied, perfumed with sour cherry, violet and pepper, fresh in acid with a gentle bitter finish; with abbacchio, the Roman milk fed lamb, and pasta all'amatriciana.
Light, dry or off dry, with green apple and almond; a lakeside white for fish from Lake Bolsena.
A sweet red scented with rose and raspberry, still or fortified as a liquoroso; with dark chocolate and berry tarts.
Montepulciano led, with Cesanese and international grapes: dark fruit, soft tannin and a medium to full body, for grilled meats and Roman offal dishes.

exam: Place both regions: Liguria on the coast around Genoa between France and Tuscany, the Valle d'Aosta in the Alps under Mont Blanc, north of Piedmont.
Know Vermentino as the lead white of the Ligurian coast and Pigato as Vermentino by DNA, bottled under its own name.
Know Sciacchetrà as the Cinque Terre's sweet wine from dried Bosco, Albarola and Vermentino, and the Cinque Terre as terraces on cliffs above the sea.
Know Rossese di Dolceacqua as a pale red of the far west and Liguria's first DOC, in 1972; Liguria has no DOCG.
Know the Valle d'Aosta as Italy's smallest wine region, with one DOC, Valle d'Aosta or Vallée d'Aoste, and no IGT.
Name the valley's grapes: Petit Rouge and Fumin red, Prié Blanc and Petite Arvine white, and Nebbiolo called Picotendro at Donnas, on stone-pillared pergolas like Carema's over the Piedmont border.
Know Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle: Prié Blanc, ungrafted, on low pergolas at up to about 1,200 metres.
The seven sub-zones and Ormeasco as Dolcetto are asked from Premier Cru; Golfo del Tigullio-Portofino and Colline di Levanto from Grand Cru.

grapes.name: Vermentino
grapes.styles: The main white of both Rivieras and of the Colli di Luni: citrus, herbs and a saline finish, mostly unoaked and drunk young.

grapes.name: Pigato
grapes.styles: Vermentino by DNA, grown as a separate vine with freckled skins on the Riviera di Ponente around Albenga; fuller and more savoury than the coast's Vermentino.

grapes.name: Bosco
grapes.styles: The lead white of the Cinque Terre, with Albarola and Vermentino, the backbone of both the dry white and the sweet Sciacchetrà.

grapes.name: Albarola
grapes.styles: A Cinque Terre and Levante white, the partner of Bosco, light and fresh.

grapes.name: Rossese
grapes.styles: The grape of Rossese di Dolceacqua in the far west, the same vine as Provence's Tibouren: pale, perfumed reds of red berries, roses and spice.

grapes.name: Dolcetto
grapes.styles: Called Ormeasco in the hills of Pornassio, where it makes a firm red and a rosé called Sciac-trà.

grapes.name: Petit Rouge
grapes.styles: The Valle d'Aosta's main red, behind Torrette and Enfer d'Arvier: light to medium bodied, with cherries, violets and a bitter almond finish.

grapes.name: Fumin
grapes.styles: A darker, firmer native red, peppery and structured, bottled alone and often aged in wood, or blended with Petit Rouge.

grapes.name: Nebbiolo
grapes.styles: Called Picotendro or Picotener in the lower valley, where it makes Donnas and Arnad-Montjovet: paler and leaner than Barolo, with rose and red cherry.

grapes.name: Prié Blanc
grapes.styles: The only grape of Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle, grown ungrafted under Mont Blanc: very light, crisp and herbal, still or sparkling.

grapes.name: Petite Arvine
grapes.styles: Shared with the Swiss Valais: a saline, high-acid white of grapefruit and herbs, increasingly planted in the valley.

grapes.name: Cornalin
grapes.styles: A native red of the valley, the vine the Valais calls Humagne Rouge, deep in colour and spicy.

grapes.name: Muscat Blanc
grapes.styles: Moscato Bianco at Chambave, made dry and as the sweet Flétri from grapes dried after picking.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Called Malvoisie at Nus, made dry or sweet from dried grapes, with a coppery tint.

law.classification: Liguria has no DOCG. Its wines are DOC or IGT: Rossese di Dolceacqua became the region's first DOC in 1972, and Cinque Terre, with Cinque Terre Sciacchetrà, followed in 1973. Riviera Ligure di Ponente is the broad DOC of the western coast, for Pigato, Vermentino, Rossese and others, and Ormeasco di Pornassio was split from it as a DOC of its own in 2003. In the east, Colli di Luni crosses the border into Tuscany, and Golfo del Tigullio-Portofino, Colline di Levanto and Val Polcevera cover the hills of the Levante and around Genoa. The Valle d'Aosta has a single DOC, Valle d'Aosta or Vallée d'Aoste, written in Italian or French, which absorbed the older Donnas and Enfer d'Arvier DOCs. Its label carries the regional name with a grape, such as Petite Arvine or Fumin, or with one of seven named sub-zones. Like Piedmont next door, the Valle d'Aosta has never registered an IGT.

Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle, Enfer d'Arvier, Torrette, Nus, Chambave, Arnad-Montjovet and Donnas, from upstream to downstream.
Rossese di Dolceacqua DOC
1972, Liguria's first DOC: Rossese red from the valleys behind Ventimiglia.
Cinque Terre and Cinque Terre Sciacchetrà DOC
1973: the dry white and the sweet passito of Bosco, Albarola and Vermentino from the cliffs east of Genoa.
Riviera Ligure di Ponente DOC
The broad DOC of the western coast, for Pigato, Vermentino, Rossese and others, with named sub-zones.
Ormeasco di Pornassio DOC

Colli di Luni DOC

IGT

made.viticulture: Both regions are farmed by hand on steep ground. In Liguria the vineyards stand on terraces held up by dry stone walls built over centuries, and many were abandoned in the twentieth century as the coast's other work paid better. At the Cinque Terre small monorail trains carry grapes and tools up and down the cliffs, and vines are kept low, on short pergolas or as bush vines, out of the wind. Yields are small and costs high. In the Valle d'Aosta the vines climb terraces on the sunny north side of the valley. At Morgex and La Salle, Prié Blanc grows ungrafted on low pergolas close to the ground, which take the warmth the stony soil stores by day through the cold nights; phylloxera never took hold at that height, and new vines are still propagated on their own roots. Lower down, at Donnas, Nebbiolo is trained on pergolas held up by stone pillars, as at Carema across the border in Piedmont. Frost, a short season and the steepness of the ground keep every harvest small.
made.winemaking: Most whites in both regions are fermented cool in steel and bottled young to keep their freshness and salinity; some Pigato and Vermentino is kept on its lees or rested in large wood for texture. Sciacchetrà is made from the ripest bunches of Bosco, Albarola and Vermentino, dried for weeks in airy lofts or on racks until the berries shrivel, then pressed late in the autumn and fermented slowly into a sweet, amber wine. In the Valle d'Aosta, Petit Rouge is made for freshness and drunk within a few years, while Fumin and Donnas take longer and often see wood. Chambave Muscat and Nus Malvoisie are also made as Flétri, the valley's French word for a wine from grapes dried after picking. Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle is made still and as a sparkling wine, including by the traditional method. Cooperatives make much of the valley's wine and keep its many small growers in business.

places.name: Riviera di Ponente
places.note: The coast west of Genoa to the French border, warmer and drier than the east, home of Pigato, Vermentino and Rossese under the broad Riviera Ligure di Ponente DOC.

places.name: Rossese di Dolceacqua
places.note: The valleys of the Nervia and its neighbours behind Ventimiglia, around the village of Dolceacqua near the French border: pale, perfumed Rossese reds, Liguria's first DOC in 1972.

places.name: Albenga
places.note: The plain and hills around Albenga in Savona province, the heartland of Pigato, whose wines are fuller and more savoury than the coast's Vermentino.

places.name: Ormeasco di Pornassio
places.note: High hills of the upper Arroscia valley in Imperia province, towards Piedmont, where Dolcetto is called Ormeasco and makes a red and the rosé Sciac-trà; a DOC of its own since 2003.

places.name: Riviera di Levante
places.note: The coast east of Genoa to Tuscany, steeper and more rugged, with Vermentino, Bosco, Albarola and Bianchetta Genovese on terraces above the sea.

places.name: Cinque Terre
places.note: Five villages on the cliffs north-west of La Spezia, Monterosso al Mare, Vernazza, Corniglia, Manarola and Riomaggiore, with terraced vineyards over the sea, worked by hand and by monorail: the dry white and the sweet Sciacchetrà.

places.name: Colli di Luni
places.note: The hills around the old Roman port of Luni at Liguria's eastern end, a DOC that crosses into Tuscany, known for full, saline Vermentino.

places.name: Golfo del Tigullio-Portofino and Colline di Levanto
places.note: Two small DOCs of the Levante hills between Genoa and the Cinque Terre, for Vermentino, Bianchetta Genovese and Ciliegiolo.

places.name: Valle d'Aosta
places.note: The Alpine valley of the Dora Baltea between Mont Blanc and Piedmont, Italy's smallest wine region, with one DOC and seven named sub-zones on the sunny north side of the valley.

places.name: Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle
places.note: The upper valley under Mont Blanc, from about 900 to 1,200 metres: ungrafted Prié Blanc on low pergolas, still or sparkling.

places.name: Enfer d'Arvier
places.note: A hot, sheltered bowl of rock at Arvier west of Aosta, whose name means hell for its summer heat; reds of Petit Rouge, once a DOC of its own.

places.name: Torrette
places.note: The communes either side of the city of Aosta, on the sunny slopes of the central valley, for reds led by Petit Rouge.

places.name: Nus
places.note: East of Aosta, for a red of the local Vien de Nus and for Malvoisie, the local name for Pinot Gris, dry or Flétri.

terroir.climate: Liguria is Mediterranean: mild winters, warm, dry summers and constant sea breezes, with the mountains at its back shutting out the cold north winds, so olives and vines share the same slopes. Rain falls mostly in autumn and can come in violent storms. The Valle d'Aosta is Alpine and continental, but the high peaks around it hold off much of the rain, so it is dry and sunny for a mountain valley, with cold winters, warm days and cool nights in summer. The wide swing from day to night keeps acidity and aroma in the grapes; spring frost and an early autumn are the hazards.
terroir.soils: Liguria's terraces are cut into poor, stony ground, mostly schist, sandstone and marl, with clay and limestone in places, built up behind dry stone walls and quick to drain. The Valle d'Aosta's vineyards lie on glacial moraine and the debris of old rockfalls over crystalline rock: sandy, stony, thin soils low in organic matter that warm quickly in the sun and drain freely.
terroir.topography: Liguria is a strip only a few kilometres deep in places, curving from the French border to Tuscany with Genoa at its centre: the Riviera di Ponente runs west of the city, the Riviera di Levante east. Slopes rise straight from the sea to the ridges, so almost every vineyard is terraced, at the Cinque Terre on cliffs above the water. The Valle d'Aosta runs east from Mont Blanc along the Dora Baltea to the narrow gap at Pont-Saint-Martin, where it opens into Piedmont. Vines grow mostly on the south-facing slopes of the valley's north side, on terraces from the valley floor up to about 1,200 metres at Morgex.
terroir.water: The Ligurian Sea, the north-western arm of the Mediterranean, warms the coast in winter and cools it in summer, and its breezes dry the vines after rain. The Dora Baltea drains the Valle d'Aosta from the glaciers of Mont Blanc east into Piedmont and on to the Po, and the cold air that slides down from the ice at night keeps the upper valley fresh.

traps: Pigato and Vermentino are one variety by DNA, though they are grown and bottled under separate names.
Sciacchetrà is the Cinque Terre's sweet passito; Sciac-trà is the dry rosé of Ormeasco di Pornassio.
Ormeasco is Dolcetto, not a separate grape.
Liguria has no DOCG; the Valle d'Aosta has one DOC and no IGT.
The Valle d'Aosta's Cornalin is the Valais's Humagne Rouge, not the Valais's own Cornalin.
Donnas and Carema both grow Nebbiolo on stone pillars, but Carema is in Piedmont, not the Valle d'Aosta.
Malvoisie at Nus is Pinot Gris, not a Malvasia.
Colli di Luni crosses the regional border: part of it lies in Tuscany.

law.classification: Franciacorta, a DOC from 1967 for still and sparkling wine, became in 1995 the first DOCG reserved for bottle-fermented sparkling wine (Trento DOC, in 1993, was the first denomination of any rank written for it alone), and it is the model: Chardonnay, Pinot Nero and Pinot Bianco (the last capped at half), with Erbamat allowed up to ten per cent since 2017; styles are defined by lees time and grape (Satèn, Rosé, Millesimato, Riserva); still wines from the same hills are Curtefranca DOC. Valtellina Superiore DOCG (1998) names five subzones and demands 90% Nebbiolo; Sforzato di Valtellina DOCG (2003) is the dried-grape red; Rosso di Valtellina DOC is the lighter wine. Oltrepò Pavese Metodo Classico DOCG (2007) covers Pinot Nero-led traditional method sparkling, while the Oltrepò's still wines stay DOC. Lugana DOC straddles the border with Veneto. Moscato di Scanzo DOCG is the smallest in the country. Lombardy, unlike Piedmont, has IGTs for everything else.

made.viticulture: Franciacorta is farmed for sparkling wine: Chardonnay and Pinot Nero picked early and by hand (hand harvest is compulsory), yields capped, Guyot and spur-pruned cordon on the moraine. The mild lake climate makes ripeness easy, so the task is keeping acidity. Valtellina is the opposite: heroic viticulture on terraces too narrow for anything but hands and, in places, a small helicopter for the crates; the dry stone walls store the day's heat, the slope faces due south, and the grapes for Sforzato are laid in airy lofts to dry through the autumn until a good part of their weight has gone. Lugana's clay and Garda's mild air allow machine work on flat ground. Oltrepò Pavese is hill country of Pinot Nero, Croatina and Barbera, farmed by cooperatives and estates alike. Hazards: hail and summer storms on the plain, frost and landslip in the valley.
made.winemaking: Franciacorta follows the Champagne sequence: gentle pressing, base wines fermented in steel or some oak, assemblage, second fermentation in the bottle of sale, lees ageing well beyond the legal floor (18 months non vintage, 24 for Satèn and Rosé, 30 for vintage, 60 for Riserva), riddling, disgorgement and dosage from Pas Dosé to Demi-Sec. Satèn is bottled to a lower pressure, under five atmospheres, and only as Brut. The law lets the name Franciacorta stand alone on the label without the words spumante or DOCG. Valtellina Superiore ages at least 24 months with 12 in wood; Sforzato takes dried grapes to a dry wine of 14% or more and ages at least 20 months. Lugana is cold fermented in steel, sometimes with lees stirring; Riserva and late-harvest versions exist. Oltrepò's Bonarda is often fermented in pressurised tank for its gentle fizz, and its Pinot Nero goes both into bottle-fermented sparkling and into still red.

places.name: Franciacorta
places.note: The hills south of Lake Iseo in the province of Brescia; Erbusco is the main village. Traditional method sparkling since 1961, when the first bottles were made at Berlucchi, then DOC in 1967 and DOCG in 1995.

places.name: Valtellina

terroir.climate: Three climates in one region. The Po plain is humid, foggy in winter and hot in summer. The lakes (Garda, Iseo, Como) store heat and soften the extremes on their shores, which is what Franciacorta and Lugana depend on. Valtellina is alpine and continental, dry, with strong sun on its south-facing wall and a sharp drop at night; the breva, a daytime breeze off Lake Como, dries the vines.
terroir.soils: Franciacorta sits on the moraine left by the Iseo glacier: deep gravel and sand mixed with limestone pebbles, free draining and warm. Valtellina's terraces are shallow, sandy, acidic soils weathered from granite and schist, held by dry stone walls. Lugana is heavy white clay of glacial origin, which gives its white weight and keeps it fresh. Oltrepò Pavese is clay and limestone in the Apennine foothills.
terroir.topography: From the Alps in the north through the lake district to the flat Po plain, then the Apennine foothills of Oltrepò across the river in the south. Franciacorta is a low amphitheatre of hills below Lake Iseo; Valtellina is an east-west valley whose north bank faces due south, terraced from the valley floor to around 700 metres; Lugana is nearly flat.
terroir.water: The Po crosses the whole south of the region; the Adda runs through Valtellina and into Lake Como; Lake Iseo warms Franciacorta and Lake Garda warms Lugana and the Valtènesi shore. Lakes rather than sea are the moderating water here.

traps: Satèn is not a sweetness level; it is a white-grape Franciacorta at lower pressure, always Brut.
Franciacorta is one of the few Italian names allowed to stand alone on the label without spumante or DOCG; do not read that as a lower tier.
Sforzato is dry; it is not Recioto and not sweet. It is Valtellina's Amarone, made from Nebbiolo, not Corvina.
Chiavennasca is Nebbiolo; the town is Chiavenna but the wine zone is Valtellina.
Lugana's grape was called Trebbiano di Lugana but DNA ties it to Verdicchio, not to the Trebbiano Toscano of Tuscany.
Bonarda in Oltrepò is Croatina; Bonarda in Alto Piemonte is Uva Rara; Argentina's Bonarda is a different grape again.
Inferno is a Valtellina subzone, not a style; the name is about heat on the slope.

wines.note: Traditional method, dry, fine mousse, apple and brioche, at least eighteen months on the lees for the basic wine; served as Champagne is, well chilled in a tall glass, with anything fried or salted.
White grapes only, lower pressure, always Brut: a silkier, softer mousse. The name was coined by the consortium and belongs to it.
Pinot Nero gives a substantial share of the blend; 24 months on the lees; red fruit and a firmer line.
At least 90% Nebbiolo with two years' ageing, from the terraced subzones: pale, floral, red fruit, firm acid and tannin, lighter than Barolo and ready sooner.
Nebbiolo dried after harvest, then fermented dry to at least 14%; the first dry dried-grape red to be DOCG, with Nebbiolo's perfume over Amarone's weight.
Turbiana: dry, medium bodied, citrus and almond with a saline edge, served cold with the lake's fish and risotto.
At least 70% Pinot Nero, bottle fermented; with Franciacorta and Alta Langa, one of Italy's traditional method DOCGs.
Croatina, soft and dark, often lightly frizzante, the carafe wine of Pavia with salami.
Groppello-led, pale, dry rosé from Garda's western shore, for lake fish and summer.
A tiny sweet red passito from a hamlet near Bergamo, rose and spice; Italy's smallest DOCG.

exam: Verdicchio is the Marche's grape: name the two DOCs the Court lists, Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi and Verdicchio di Matelica, and know that the Riserva of each became a DOCG in 2010.
Tell the zones apart: Castelli di Jesi in the hills west of Ancona, open to the sea; Matelica in a high inland valley running north to south, cooler and continental.
Verdicchio is the same variety as Trebbiano di Soave and so close to Lugana's Turbiana in DNA studies that the two are often taught as one; no relation of Trebbiano Toscano.
Montepulciano leads the reds: Rosso Conero and the Conero DOCG on the limestone headland, Rosso Piceno blended with Sangiovese.
Climate: maritime on the coast and continental inland, the Court's category for central Italy; the Apennines to the west and the Adriatic to the east.
Superiore on a label means a higher minimum alcohol; Riserva means longer ageing.
From Premier Cru, know Offida for Pecorino and Passerina, and Vernaccia di Serrapetrona as a sparkling red.

grapes.name: Verdicchio
grapes.styles: The region's white, named for its green tinge: high acid, lemon, green almond and a bitter almond finish, and it ages well, gaining honey and nut over a decade or more. DNA ties it to Trebbiano di Soave and to Lugana's Turbiana.

grapes.name: Montepulciano
grapes.styles: The red of the Conero and the base of Rosso Piceno: deep colour, plum and black cherry, soft acid and firm, ripe tannin.

grapes.name: Sangiovese
grapes.styles: Blended with Montepulciano in Rosso Piceno, in Rosso Conero and in many IGT reds, where it adds acid and red cherry fruit.

grapes.name: Pecorino
grapes.styles: A mountain white revived in the south of the region and in Abruzzo: early ripening, high in acid and alcohol, with herbs, citrus and a stony edge; one of the Offida DOCG's whites.

grapes.name: Passerina
grapes.styles: A productive white of the south, fresh and citrusy, made still, sparkling and passito; the second white of the Offida DOCG.

grapes.name: Lacrima
grapes.styles: A red of Morro d'Alba near Ancona, strongly scented of rose and violet, soft and juicy.

grapes.name: Vernaccia Nera
grapes.styles: The red of Serrapetrona, made into a sparkling red from partly dried grapes, dry or sweet.

grapes.name: Bianchello
grapes.styles: Biancame by its variety name, the light, crisp white of the Metauro valley in the north.

law.classification: In 2026 the Marche holds five DOCGs, a longer list of DOCs and the Marche IGT. The Court names the two Verdicchio DOCs, Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi and Verdicchio di Matelica, at least 85 per cent Verdicchio. In 2010 the Riserva of each was raised to DOCG, as Castelli di Jesi Verdicchio Riserva, Jesi's name reordered, and Verdicchio di Matelica Riserva. The Conero DOCG of 2004 is the Riserva level of Rosso Conero, at least 85 per cent Montepulciano. Offida is the DOCG of the south for Pecorino, Passerina and a Montepulciano led red, and Vernaccia di Serrapetrona the DOCG of a sparkling red. Among the DOCs, Rosso Piceno blends Montepulciano with Sangiovese, and Lacrima di Morro d'Alba is a scented red. On the labels, Classico marks the historic core of the Jesi zone, Superiore a higher minimum alcohol and Riserva longer ageing.

made.viticulture: Most vineyards sit on hill slopes, trained on Guyot or spurred cordon at moderate density. Verdicchio is vigorous and productive, so quality growers hold back the crop and pick when acid and ripeness balance. The Castelli di Jesi, nearer the sea, ripen earlier than the higher, cooler Matelica valley, where the harvest runs later and the wines keep more acid. Montepulciano ripens late and needs the warm, sunny slopes of the Conero and the south; Pecorino, early ripening, suits the higher sites of the Piceno. The hazards are spring frost in the inland valleys, summer drought and hail, and rain at harvest on the coast.
made.winemaking: Verdicchio is mostly fermented cool in stainless steel and bottled young, but the grape rewards time: many Riserva wines rest on their fine lees for months, some in large old casks and a few in barrique, and they keep for many years. Verdicchio also makes traditional method and tank sparkling wine and a sweet passito. Montepulciano for Conero is macerated for colour and tannin and aged in large casks or barrique, at least two years for the DOCG. Rosso Piceno blends Montepulciano with Sangiovese and ages longer for Superiore. Vernaccia di Serrapetrona is made unusually: part of the grapes is dried for weeks, the fresh grapes are fermented, the must of the dried grapes is added for a second fermentation, and a third fermentation, mostly in pressure tank, makes the sparkle.

places.name: Castelli di Jesi
places.note: The hills west of Ancona on both banks of the Esino, named for the walled hill towns, the castelli, around Jesi: the larger Verdicchio zone, nearer the sea, with Classico covering its historic core.

places.name: Cupramontana and Staffolo
places.note: Hill towns on the higher right bank of the Esino, among the zone's cooler sites, whose Verdicchio is taut and slow to age.

places.name: Matelica
places.note: A high inland valley in the Apennines, running north to south between two ridges and closed to the sea, so its climate is continental with cold nights; its Verdicchio is leaner, sharper and slower to open than Jesi's.

places.name: Conero
places.note: Monte Conero, a limestone headland rising straight from the Adriatic south of Ancona, whose slopes grow Montepulciano for Rosso Conero and the Conero DOCG.

places.name: Piceno
places.note: The hills of the south around Ascoli Piceno, home of Rosso Piceno, a blend of Montepulciano and Sangiovese, with its Superiore from a smaller area near Ascoli.

places.name: Offida
places.note: A hill town north of Ascoli whose DOCG covers Pecorino, Passerina and a Montepulciano led Rosso.

places.name: Morro d'Alba
places.note: A village in the hills north-west of Ancona, home of the scented red Lacrima di Morro d'Alba.

places.name: Serrapetrona
places.note: A hill village in the province of Macerata whose DOCG makes Vernaccia Nera into a sparkling red, dry or sweet, by three fermentations.

places.name: Bianchello del Metauro
places.note: The Metauro valley inland from Fano in the north of the region, a DOC for the light white Bianchello, Biancame by its variety name.

producers.name: Bucci
producers.why: A Castelli di Jesi estate whose Villa Bucci Riserva, matured in large old casks, makes the case for Verdicchio as a white to age.

producers.name: La Monacesca
producers.why: A Matelica estate whose Mirum Riserva shows the tighter, slower inland Verdicchio.

producers.name: Fazi Battaglia
producers.why: A Castelli di Jesi house whose amphora shaped bottle carried Verdicchio abroad in the decades after the Second World War.

producers.name: Garofoli
producers.why: An old family house of Loreto known for Verdicchio, sparkling wines among them, and for Grosso Agontano, a Conero Riserva.

producers.name: Saladini Pilastri
producers.why: An old family estate of the Piceno, farmed organically, known for Rosso Piceno Superiore and Offida Pecorino.

producers.name: Velenosi
producers.why: An Ascoli Piceno house known for Rosso Piceno Superiore and for the Offida whites, Pecorino and Passerina.

terroir.climate: The Court files central Italy as maritime on the coast and continental inland, and the Marche shows both within a short drive. The coast and the low hills are warmed by the Adriatic and aired by its breezes, with hot, dry summers and mild winters; inland, under the Apennines, winters are colder, nights cooler and the swing between day and night wider. Matelica, shut off from the sea, is the continental pole of the region, Jesi and the Conero the maritime one.
terroir.soils: Clay and limestone over sandstone and marl cover most of the hills, laid down as seabed and lifted with the Apennines. The Castelli di Jesi hold calcareous clay and sandstone, with sand on some higher ridges; the Matelica valley has more limestone and gravel. The Conero is a block of limestone rising from the sea, and the southern hills around Ascoli and Offida are clay and sand.
terroir.topography: A comb of parallel valleys runs from the Apennine ridge east to the Adriatic, each with its river, so the land rises in a series of hill crests from the coast towards mountains of over 2,000 metres. Monte Conero, south of Ancona, is the one real headland on a long, straight coast. Matelica is the exception to the comb: a valley running north to south between two Apennine ridges, with no opening to the sea.
terroir.water: The rivers are short and parallel: the Esino, whose valley holds the Castelli di Jesi and names the Esino DOC, the Musone, the Potenza, the Chienti, the Tenna and the Tronto on the Abruzzo border. The Adriatic tempers the coast and the lower hills, and the Esino valley carries sea air inland towards Jesi.

traps: Montepulciano here is the grape, as in Abruzzo; Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is Sangiovese from a Tuscan town.
The Court lists the Verdicchio zones as DOCs; the DOCG belongs only to the Riserva wines, named Castelli di Jesi Verdicchio Riserva and Verdicchio di Matelica Riserva.
Matelica is the smaller, higher and inland zone; Castelli di Jesi is the larger one, nearer the sea.
Vernaccia di Serrapetrona is a red sparkling wine from Vernaccia Nera, unrelated to the white Vernaccia di San Gimignano of Tuscany.
Pecorino is a white grape of the Marche and Abruzzo as well as a sheep's cheese.
Lacrima di Morro d'Alba is a red of the Marche, nothing to do with Alba in Piedmont.
The Conero DOCG is the Riserva level; plain Rosso Conero stays a DOC.

wines.note: Straw with green glints, lemon, green apple, fennel and almond, dry and fresh with a bitter almond finish; with brodetto fish soup, fried seafood and crudo.
wines.style: Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi Classico

wines.note: Riper and longer aged, gaining honey, beeswax and toasted almond over the years; it stands up to white meats, mushrooms and truffle dishes.
Tighter and more mineral than Jesi, with citrus, flint and a saline bite; it opens slowly and repays a few years in bottle.
Montepulciano from the headland, dark and plummy with firm tannin and an earthy, savoury finish; with lamb, game and aged pecorino cheese.
Montepulciano softened by Sangiovese: cherry, plum and dried herbs, medium bodied and ready young; with the stuffed fried olives of Ascoli and grilled meats.
Full and fresh, with sage, citrus and a stony, savoury finish; with grilled fish and young sheep's cheese.
A sparkling red, dry or sweet, with red berries, pepper and a faint bitter edge; the dry version with salumi, the sweet one with dry pastries.
Perfumed with rose, violet and strawberry, soft and juicy; serve it lightly cool with charcuterie or a fish soup.

The five core Barolo communes and the Tortonian versus Serravallian split; the three Barbaresco communes.
Nebbiolo's synonyms by place: Spanna, Chiavennasca, Picotendro.
The grape behind each place name: Gavi is Cortese, Roero's white is Arneis, Asti and Moscato d'Asti are Moscato Bianco, Nizza is Barbera, Dogliani is Dolcetto, Acqui is Brachetto.
Moscato d'Asti: tank method, stopped fermentation, around five per cent alcohol, frizzante not spumante.

grapes.name: Nebbiolo
grapes.styles: Barolo and Barbaresco in the Langhe, Roero across the river, and the lighter alpine wines of Gattinara, Ghemme and Carema, where it goes by Spanna or Picotendro. Pale colour, tar and rose, high acid and among the firmest tannins in Italy.

grapes.name: Barbera
grapes.styles: The most planted red of the region and its daily glass: deep colour, high acid, low tannin, sour cherry. Barbera d'Asti and Nizza are the serious DOCGs, Barbera d'Alba the plusher Langhe version.

grapes.name: Dolcetto
grapes.styles: The early-ripening, soft, dry red that takes the cooler sites Nebbiolo refuses; Dogliani, Diano d'Alba and Ovada give it DOCG status, Dolcetto d'Alba the everyday bottle.

grapes.name: Muscat Blanc
grapes.styles: Moscato Bianco makes Moscato d'Asti, gently frizzante and sweet near five per cent alcohol, and the fully sparkling Asti; Canelli is the historic heart and since 2023 its own DOCG.

grapes.name: Cortese
grapes.styles: The white of Gavi in the south-east: lean, citrus, mineral, dry and unoaked, built for the seafood of the Ligurian coast next door.

grapes.name: Arneis
grapes.styles: Roero's white, rescued from near extinction in the 1970s: pear, white flowers, soft acid and a faint bitterness on the finish.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: With Pinot Nero, the base of Alta Langa, the region's traditional method sparkling DOCG, and of some oaked Langhe whites.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Pinot Nero partners Chardonnay in Alta Langa and appears in a few cool Langhe DOC reds.

grapes.name: Brachetto
grapes.styles: A sweet, aromatic, frothy red from Acqui: strawberry and rose, low alcohol, the region's answer to a bowl of berries.

grapes.name: Grignolino
grapes.styles: Pale, tannic and peppery red of Monferrato and Asti, an old local taste served cool.

grapes.name: Freisa
grapes.styles: A relative of Nebbiolo making strawberry-scented, tannic reds, still or lightly fizzy, around Asti and Chieri.

grapes.name: Ruchè
grapes.styles: An aromatic red of Castagnole Monferrato, rose and spice, with its own DOCG since 2010.

grapes.name: Erbaluce
grapes.styles: Canavese's high-acid white, made dry, sparkling or dried for Caluso Passito.

grapes.name: Timorasso
grapes.styles: The Colli Tortonesi white revived from a handful of vines: full, waxy, long-lived, often labelled Derthona.

law.classification: Piedmont has no IGT; every bottle is DOCG, DOC or plain vino, and the region holds more DOCGs than any other. The ladder reads from the broad Piemonte DOC, through Langhe and Monferrato DOC, to village denominations and the DOCGs. Barolo and Barbaresco are the model: a single grape, a mapped zone of named communes, ageing minimums counted from the first of November after harvest, and since 2007 and 2010 the Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive, the official vineyard names a label may add: 181 in Barolo (170 vineyards plus the eleven communes), 66 in Barbaresco. Riserva means longer ageing, Superiore higher alcohol, Vigna a named site inside an MGA held to a lower yield.
labels: Barolo 62 months, Barbaresco 50 months, each with the same wood minimum as the base wine
A higher minimum alcohol and often extra ageing, as in Barbera d'Asti Superiore
An official vineyard name on a Barolo or Barbaresco label: Cannubi, Brunate, Asili
A single named vineyard inside an MGA, from vines of a minimum age at a lower yield
Langhe dialect for a sunny, south-facing slope, used in vineyard names
A hilltop; another word that appears in vineyard names
Barolo aromatised with quinine bark, a bitter digestivo
Nebbiolo's name in Alto Piemonte; Chiavennasca in Valtellina, Picotendro in Carema

Barolo, Barbaresco, Roero, Gavi, Asti and Moscato d'Asti, Barbera d'Asti, Nizza, Dogliani, Gattinara, Ghemme, Brachetto d'Acqui, Alta Langa, Ruchè di Castagnole Monferrato, Erbaluce di Caluso, Terre Alfieri (2020) and Canelli (2023) among them; each tasted and sealed by the state

Langhe, Piemonte, Monferrato and the village DOCs: Barbera d'Alba, Dolcetto d'Alba, Nebbiolo d'Alba, Langhe Nebbiolo, Carema, Lessona, Boca, Bramaterra, Colli Tortonesi

Everything else; Piedmont, like the Valle d'Aosta beside it, has never registered an IGT

made.viticulture: Nebbiolo buds early and ripens late, so it takes the warmest, best-drained south-facing slopes and everything else takes the cooler aspects: Dolcetto the higher or north-facing sites, Barbera the mid slopes, Moscato the chalky hills around Canelli. Vines are mostly Guyot trained, and the hills are largely picked by hand on slopes too steep for machines. Frost at budbreak, summer hail and rain during the long Nebbiolo harvest are the hazards; Barolo growers watch the sky through October while Dolcetto is already in the cellar. Barolo's rules cap the crop at eight tonnes per hectare and keep Nebbiolo to the hillsides. The MGA system, mapped in Barbaresco in 2007 and Barolo in 2010, lets a bottle name its vineyard, so single-site farming has grown. In Carema, terraces and pergolas on stone pillars lift the vines off the cold ground.
made.winemaking: The old way: long macerations of several weeks, sometimes under a submerged cap, then years in large Slavonian oak botti that let the wine breathe without tasting of wood. The modern way, which arrived in the 1980s: shorter, warmer macerations, rotary fermenters, and ageing in French barriques for colour, softness and earlier appeal. Most houses now sit between the two. The law sets the floor: Barolo must age 38 months from the November after harvest, 18 of them in wood, 62 months for Riserva; Barbaresco 26 months with 9 in wood, 50 for Riserva. Barbera is often given barrique to tame its acid; Dolcetto is kept fresh in steel. Moscato d'Asti is a tank wine whose single fermentation is stopped by chilling and filtration with sugar still in it, which is why it is so low in alcohol. Barolo Chinato infuses finished Barolo with china bark, sugar and spices.

places.name: Langhe
places.note: The hills south of the Tanaro around Alba, home to Barolo, Barbaresco and the white truffle. Langhe DOC is the broad net (Langhe Nebbiolo, Langhe Chardonnay); Dogliani and Diano d'Alba are its Dolcetto DOCGs.

places.name: Barolo
places.note: Eleven communes south-west of Alba, five of which hold most of the vineyard: La Morra and Barolo on the softer Tortonian marl to the west, Castiglione Falletto, Serralunga d'Alba and Monforte d'Alba on the harder Serravallian ground to the east. All Nebbiolo, 38 months with 18 in wood, 13% minimum.

places.name: La Morra
places.note: The largest commune and the most perfumed Barolo, on Tortonian marl: Brunate (shared with Barolo village), Cerequio, Rocche dell'Annunziata, Arborina.

places.name: Barolo (village)
places.note: The commune that names the wine: Cannubi, the most famous hill, with Sarmassa and lower Brunate.

places.name: Castiglione Falletto
places.note: Both soils meet in the centre of the zone: Monprivato, Villero, Rocche di Castiglione, Bricco Boschis.

places.name: Serralunga d'Alba
places.note: The eastern ridge on Serravallian sandstone and marl, the most tannic and longest-lived Barolo: Vigna Rionda, Francia, Lazzarito, Falletto.

places.name: Monforte d'Alba
places.note: The south-east, powerful and dark: Bussia, Ginestra, Mosconi, Santo Stefano di Perno.

places.name: Barbaresco
places.note: Three communes north-east of Alba, Barbaresco, Neive and Treiso, plus a sliver of Alba itself. Lower, nearer the Tanaro and mostly on Tortonian soils, so the Nebbiolo ripens a week or two earlier and the wine opens sooner: 26 months with 9 in wood, 12.5% minimum.

places.name: Barbaresco (village)
places.note: Asili, Rabajà, Martinenga, Montestefano and Pora, with the Gaja house's Sorì Tildìn and Sorì San Lorenzo.

places.name: Neive
places.note: Fuller, more structured Barbaresco from the north-east: Santo Stefano, Gallina, Basarin, Currà.

places.name: Treiso
places.note: The highest and coolest of the three, the most delicate wines: Pajorè, Bernadot, Marcarini.

places.name: Dogliani
places.note: The Dolcetto DOCG south of Barolo, where the grape is taken seriously enough to age a few years.

places.name: Alba
places.note: The town at the centre of the Langhe; Nebbiolo d'Alba, Barbera d'Alba and Dolcetto d'Alba cover the wider hills and Roero.

places.name: Roero
places.note: The left bank of the Tanaro north of Alba, sand over marl, steeper and more eroded than the Langhe. DOCG since 2004 for Roero (lighter, earlier Nebbiolo) and Roero Arneis.

places.name: Monferrato
places.note: The rolling hills east of the Langhe between Asti and Casale, Barbera's homeland: Barbera d'Asti DOCG, Barbera del Monferrato, Grignolino, Freisa and Ruchè di Castagnole Monferrato, with the Moscato hills around Canelli.

places.name: Asti and Canelli
places.note: Asti DOCG covers both the fully sparkling Asti and the frizzante Moscato d'Asti; Canelli is the cellar town of the sparkling trade and since 2023 a Moscato DOCG in its own name.

places.name: Nizza
places.note: All Barbera from Nizza Monferrato and its neighbours, carved out of Barbera d'Asti as its own DOCG in 2014, with longer ageing.

places.name: Acqui
places.note: Brachetto d'Acqui DOCG, the sweet sparkling red, and Dolcetto d'Acqui; the spa town lies south-east towards Liguria.

places.name: Gavi
places.note: The south-eastern corner near the Ligurian border, limestone and clay, where Cortese makes the dry white Gavi, DOCG since 1998. Gavi di Gavi means fruit from the commune of Gavi itself.

places.name: Alto Piemonte
places.note: The hills north of Novara and Vercelli below Monte Rosa, on volcanic porphyry and glacial moraine. Nebbiolo is Spanna here, blended with Vespolina and Uva Rara into lighter, high-acid, mineral reds; Lessona, Bramaterra, Boca, Fara and Sizzano are the DOCs of the revival.

places.name: Gattinara
places.note: DOCG since 1990: at least 90% Nebbiolo, 35 months' ageing, from the hills above the town.

places.name: Ghemme
places.note: DOCG since 1997 across the Sesia in the province of Novara: at least 85% Nebbiolo, 34 months' ageing.

places.name: Canavese and Carema
places.note: North of Turin at the mouth of the Aosta valley: Carema DOC trains Nebbiolo, here Picotendro, on pergolas over stone pillars; Erbaluce di Caluso DOCG makes dry, sparkling and passito whites.

places.name: Colli Tortonesi
places.note: Hills around Tortona in the far east, where Timorasso was revived; the wine is often sold as Derthona, the town's Roman name.

places.name: Alta Langa
places.note: The high hills south of the Langhe above 250 metres, DOCG since 2011 for traditional method sparkling from Pinot Nero and Chardonnay, vintage only, at least 30 months on the lees.

producers.name: Gaja
producers.why: The Barbaresco house, founded 1859, that took Piedmont to the world market with single-vineyard bottlings and barrique; Sorì Tildìn and Sorì San Lorenzo are its names.

producers.name: Bruno Giacosa
producers.why: Neive house famed for a classic hand in both Barbaresco (Santo Stefano, Asili) and Barolo (Falletto); the red label marks its Riserva.

producers.name: Giacomo Conterno
producers.why: Monforte's keeper of the traditional school; Monfortino Riserva is the longest-aged and most sought-after Barolo.

producers.name: Bartolo Mascarello
producers.why: Barolo village traditionalist blending four vineyards into one wine in large old casks: no barrique, no single-vineyard labels.

producers.name: Giuseppe Rinaldi
producers.why: Another Barolo village traditionalist, long macerations and blended crus; Brunate and Tre Tine.

producers.name: Produttori del Barbaresco
producers.why: The village cooperative of Barbaresco, founded 1958, a benchmark for price and purity, with single-vineyard Riserve in good years.

producers.name: Vietti
producers.why: Castiglione Falletto house that pioneered single-vineyard Barolo in the 1960s and replanted Arneis; Rocche di Castiglione, Lazzarito, Ravera.

producers.name: G.D. Vajra
producers.why: The highest vineyards of Barolo commune at Vergne; Bricco delle Viole, plus a rare Freisa and a Riesling.

producers.name: Luciano Sandrone
producers.why: Modern-leaning Barolo from Cannubi Boschis, now labelled Aleste, and the blended Le Vigne.

producers.name: Giuseppe Mascarello e Figlio
producers.why: Monprivato in Castiglione Falletto, a near monopole and one of the great traditional single-vineyard Barolos.

producers.name: Cappellano
producers.why: Serralunga house that created Barolo Chinato in the late nineteenth century and still farms a plot of ungrafted Nebbiolo.

producers.name: Poderi Aldo Conterno
producers.why: Monforte house on the Bussia hill: Granbussia Riserva, Cicala, Colonnello and Romirasco.

producers.name: Massolino
producers.why: Serralunga's Vigna Rionda Riserva, classical and long-lived.

producers.name: Cavallotto
producers.why: Castiglione Falletto's Bricco Boschis, a monopole farmed organically with long cask ageing.

producers.name: Fontanafredda
producers.why: The historic Serralunga estate on land bought in 1858 by Vittorio Emanuele II, the king who went on to unite Italy; long the largest single Barolo estate.

producers.name: Pio Cesare
producers.why: Alba merchant house founded 1881 with cellars inside the town's Roman walls, blending across Barolo and Barbaresco.

producers.name: Renato Ratti
producers.why: La Morra house whose founder drew the first map of Barolo's crus in the 1970s; Marcenasco.

producers.name: Domenico Clerico
producers.why: Monforte modernist of the 1980s; Ciabot Mentin from the Ginestra hill.

producers.name: Roagna
producers.why: Barbaresco traditionalist with old vines, very long macerations and late releases; Pajè.

producers.name: Marchesi di Grésy
producers.why: Owner of the whole Martinenga amphitheatre in Barbaresco, a monopole.

producers.name: La Spinetta
producers.why: Moscato roots in Castagnole Lanze, then modern Barbaresco and Barolo under the rhinoceros label.

producers.name: Braida
producers.why: The Monferrato house that put Barbera in barrique with Bricco dell'Uccellone in 1982 and made the grape serious.

producers.name: La Miraja
producers.why: Castagnole Monferrato estate for Barbera d'Asti and the aromatic Ruchè.

producers.name: La Scolca
producers.why: The Gavi house whose black label Gavi dei Gavi made Cortese famous.

producers.name: Saracco
producers.why: Castiglione Tinella grower house regarded as the reference for Moscato d'Asti.

producers.name: Antoniolo
producers.why: Gattinara's leading estate, single-vineyard Spanna from Osso San Grato and San Francesco.

producers.name: Travaglini
producers.why: Gattinara house known for its bent bottle and long-aged Riserva.

producers.name: Proprietà Sperino
producers.why: The estate that revived Lessona and with it Alto Piemonte's reputation.

terroir.climate: Continental and sheltered: the Alps to the north and west block Atlantic weather and the Apennines close the south, so winters are cold, summers hot and dry, and autumns long, still and foggy. Nebbiolo needs that long tail; it is picked in October, weeks after Dolcetto and Barbera.
terroir.soils: The Langhe is marine marl laid down when this was sea floor. Around La Morra and the village of Barolo the Tortonian marls are bluish, calcareous and fertile, giving perfume and softer tannin. Around Serralunga, Monforte and Castiglione Falletto the older Serravallian formations carry more sandstone and compacted sand, giving denser, longer-lived wine. Roero across the Tanaro is sand; Alto Piemonte is volcanic porphyry and glacial moraine; Gavi is clay over limestone.
terroir.topography: Hill country throughout. Barolo's vineyards sit between roughly 200 and 500 metres on steep slopes south-west of Alba; Barbaresco lies lower and a little warmer to the north-east, so it ripens earlier. The best Nebbiolo sites are the south and south-west facing amphitheatres the Langhe calls sorì. Monferrato rolls lower and softer to the east around Asti; Alto Piemonte climbs towards Monte Rosa.
terroir.water: The Tanaro runs past Alba, the Langhe on its right bank and the Roero on its left; the Po drains the region eastward. No sea or lake moderates the climate, so fog settles in the valleys each autumn.

traps: Nebbiolo looks light in the glass; it is not light in the mouth. Pale garnet with high acid and high tannin is the tell.
Barbaresco is not a lesser Barolo; it is the same grape from lower, earlier-ripening hills with shorter minimums.
Barbera has high acid and low tannin; Dolcetto has low acid and moderate tannin; Nebbiolo has both high. Do not swap them.
Asti is the fully sparkling wine; Moscato d'Asti is frizzante and lower in alcohol. Both are Moscato Bianco, neither is Muscat of Alexandria.
Gavi is a town and Cortese its grape; Dolcetto means little sweet one but the wine is dry.
The Tanaro: Langhe on the right bank, Roero on the left; Barbaresco is north-east of Alba, Barolo south-west.
Gattinara and Ghemme are Nebbiolo DOCGs of Alto Piemonte, not of the Langhe, and the grape there may be blended.
The old course note called the climate simply continental; add the autumn fog and the Alpine shelter, which are what make the harvest so late.

wines.note: Pale garnet, tar, dried rose, liquorice and truffle over high acid and grippy tannin; it needs years and a big glass. Decant, serve near 17 degrees, with braised beef, truffle dishes or aged cheese.
Nebbiolo from lower, warmer hills north-east of Alba: the same aromatics in a slightly gentler frame with an earlier window. Roast game birds and mushroom risotto suit it.
Bright violet colour, sour cherry and plum, acid high enough to cut through tomato sauce, pork and salumi; little tannin, so it can be served slightly cool.
Soft, dark, dry, with blackberry and bitter almond; the first red opened on a Piedmontese table, drunk young and often.
Cortese: dry, light, lemon and green apple with a stony finish; served cold with raw fish and shellfish.
Pear, chamomile and almond with moderate acid; a rounder white than Gavi for antipasti and vitello tonnato.
Gently frizzante, sweet, grapey and floral at around five per cent alcohol; served cold with fruit, panettone or hazelnut cake, or on its own. Asti is its fully sparkling sibling.
Alto Piemonte Nebbiolo from volcanic soil: lighter in body, higher in acid, with iron and dried flowers; earlier to drink than Barolo.
Traditional method, Pinot Nero and Chardonnay, always vintage dated with at least thirty months on the lees: toasty, dry and serious.
Barolo infused with quinine bark, spices and sugar: a bitter-sweet digestivo poured in small glasses with dark chocolate.

exam: Primitivo is Zinfandel: the same vine, proved by DNA, and the same again as Croatia's Crljenak Kaštelanski or Tribidrag; Manduria and Gioia del Colle are its homes.
Negroamaro is the grape of the Salento and of Salice Salentino DOC (1976), with Malvasia Nera; the rosato tradition dates from 1943.
The four DOCGs of 2011: Castel del Monte Nero di Troia Riserva, Castel del Monte Rosso Riserva, Castel del Monte Bombino Nero (a rosato) and Primitivo di Manduria Dolce Naturale (sweet).
Dry Primitivo di Manduria is a DOC of 1974, Riserva two years; the DOCG is the sweet wine only.
Nero di Troia, also Uva di Troia, is the structured red of the north; Bombino Bianco and Nero are the north's pale grapes.
Puglia's geography: the flattest region, two seas, the Murge plateau, terra rossa over limestone, alberello bush vines, the tanker trade.
Locorotondo and Martina Franca whites from Verdeca in the Valle d'Itria.

grapes.name: Primitivo
grapes.styles: The early ripener, named for it, and the same vine as California's Zinfandel and Croatia's Tribidrag: inky, jammy blackberry and plum, high in alcohol, soft in tannin; Manduria on sand gives the richest wines, Gioia del Colle on the Murge the freshest.

grapes.name: Zinfandel
grapes.styles: The Californian name for Primitivo: the exam wants the identity, proved by DNA in the 1990s, and the Croatian name Crljenak Kaštelanski, now Tribidrag, which is the same vine again under its oldest name, not a parent.

grapes.name: Negroamaro
grapes.styles: The black bitter grape of the Salento: dark, plum and dried fig with a bitter, herbal finish and softer tannin than its colour suggests; the base of Salice Salentino and of the region's famous rosato.

grapes.name: Nero di Troia
grapes.styles: Uva di Troia, the late ripening red of the north around Castel del Monte: firmer tannin and higher acidity than the two southern grapes, with violets and black fruit; two of the three Castel del Monte DOCGs are built on it.

grapes.name: Malvasia Nera
grapes.styles: The aromatic dark partner of Negroamaro in Salice Salentino and the Salento reds, adding perfume and softness.

grapes.name: Bombino Nero
grapes.styles: A pale, thin skinned red of the Murge made into the Castel del Monte Bombino Nero rosato, the only DOCG in Italy given to a rosato alone.

grapes.name: Bombino Bianco
grapes.styles: The neutral, high yielding white of the north, once shipped as base wine and now made as a crisp dry white under Castel del Monte and San Severo.

grapes.name: Verdeca
grapes.styles: The white of the Valle d'Itria, in the light wines of Locorotondo and Martina Franca with Bianco d'Alessano.

grapes.name: Susumaniello
grapes.styles: A once vanishing red of Brindisi, deep in colour and juicy, revived as a varietal wine and in rosato.

grapes.name: Fiano
grapes.styles: Grown in the Salento for aromatic whites; the muscat scented Fiano Minutolo of the Valle d'Itria is a separate variety, Minutolo, despite the name.

law.classification: Puglia holds four DOCGs, all granted in 2011: three in the north under the Castel del Monte name, Castel del Monte Nero di Troia Riserva, Castel del Monte Rosso Riserva and Castel del Monte Bombino Nero, the last a rosato; and Primitivo di Manduria Dolce Naturale, the sweet red of the Ionian coast. The dry Primitivo di Manduria is a DOC of 1974, with a Riserva. Salice Salentino, a DOC since 1976, is the Negroamaro appellation of the Salento, alongside Brindisi, Copertino, Squinzano, Leverano, Nardò, Alezio and Lizzano. Gioia del Colle DOC holds the Murge Primitivo; Castel del Monte DOC the wider range below its DOCGs; Locorotondo and Martina Franca the Valle d'Itria whites; San Severo and Cacc'e Mmitte di Lucera the Daunia in the north; Moscato di Trani and Aleatico di Puglia the old sweet wines. The IGTs of Salento, Puglia, Tarantino, Murgia, Valle d'Itria and Daunia carry most of the varietal bottlings.

made.viticulture: The old Puglian vineyard is the alberello, the free standing bush vine pruned low to the ground that shades its own fruit and survives drought without irrigation; the oldest Primitivo and Negroamaro of Manduria and the Salento still stand this way, some of them on their own roots in the sand, and the best estates buy or rent them. Most of the plain was replanted in the twentieth century to tendone pergolas for table grapes and volume, and to cordon systems for the co-operatives; irrigation, once banned in the DOCs, is now permitted and necessary in a dry summer. Primitivo lives up to its name and is picked from mid August, often in two passes because the same vine carries a second, later crop; Negroamaro follows in September and Nero di Troia in October. The region's enemies are heat and drought rather than rot, so organic farming is easy, but sunburn and raisining on the vine are real, which is where the sweet Dolce Naturale and the old Primitivo style of over fifteen per cent began. Altitude on the Murge at Gioia del Colle and Castel del Monte gives cooler nights and fresher wines than the Salento can.
made.winemaking: For most of its history Puglia made deep, alcoholic wine to be shipped north in bulk and blended into thinner reds, and much of the region's volume still leaves in tankers or as concentrated must. The bottled wines changed from the 1990s, when northern money arrived and the co-operatives learned to control fermentation temperature in a hot September. Primitivo is fermented warm and quickly, its sugar often leaving a few grams of residual sweetness that the style embraces, and aged in large oak or barrique for the Riserva; the Dolce Naturale is fermented from overripe or dried fruit until the yeast stops in the sugar. Negroamaro is macerated for a week or so and kept away from new wood by the traditional houses so that its bitter edge reads as herb rather than tannin; a Salento rosato is made by bleeding the vat after a night on the skins, a method the region has bottled since 1943. Nero di Troia takes a longer maceration and two years for the DOCG Riserva. Verdeca whites are cool fermented in steel and bottled young. Appassimento of Primitivo and Negroamaro for dry, off dry and sweet reds is a growing local habit.

places.name: Salento
places.note: The peninsula of the heel between two seas, flat, hot and windy, home of Negroamaro, old alberello vines and the rosato tradition; Lecce, Brindisi and the southern half of Taranto province make it up, and Salento IGT is its label.

places.name: Salice Salentino
places.note: A village north of Lecce and the Negroamaro DOC of 1976 named for it, the Salento's most exported red; Leone de Castris, founded 1665, is its historic house and bottled Italy's first rosato there in 1943.

places.name: Manduria
places.note: A town on the Ionian side of Taranto province whose sandy, iron red soils and old bush vines gave Primitivo its DOC in 1974 and its sweet Dolce Naturale DOCG in 2011.

places.name: Brindisi and Copertino
places.note: Two further Negroamaro DOCs of the Salento, Brindisi on the Adriatic port and Copertino inland near Lecce, both with Riserva reds and rosato.

places.name: Gioia del Colle and the Murge
places.note: The limestone plateau between Bari and Taranto at around 300 to 500 metres, where Primitivo was first named in the late eighteenth century by a priest of Gioia del Colle; its DOC of 1987 gives the freshest Primitivo in Puglia.

places.name: Castel del Monte
places.note: The thirteenth century octagonal castle of Frederick II on the northern Murge near Andria gives its name to a DOC and, since 2011, three DOCGs built on Nero di Troia and the Bombino Nero rosato; Rivera is the house most associated with it.

places.name: Valle d'Itria
places.note: The trulli country around Locorotondo and Martina Franca, the one corner of Puglia known for white wine, light and dry from Verdeca and Bianco d'Alessano, with a sparkling tradition.

places.name: Daunia and the Tavoliere
places.note: The north of the region around Foggia: the flat Tavoliere plain, the Gargano promontory, the San Severo DOC and Cacc'e Mmitte di Lucera, with Nero di Troia, Montepulciano and Bombino Bianco; the Daunia IGT.

producers.name: Fino
producers.why: A Manduria estate sold under its founder's full name, whose Es, from old alberello Primitivo vines, is the region's most sought after red and proved that Manduria could be fine rather than merely big.

producers.name: Rivera
producers.why: The Castel del Monte house of 1950 that championed Nero di Troia with its Il Falcone Riserva and was a leading voice for the DOCGs of 2011.

producers.name: Leone de Castris
producers.why: The Salice Salentino estate founded in 1665 that bottled Italy's first rosato, Five Roses, in 1943 and made Salice Salentino a name abroad.

producers.name: Tormaresca
producers.why: The Antinori family's Puglian estates at Castel del Monte (Bocca di Lupo) and in the Salento (Masseria Maìme), part of the 1990s investment that changed the region.

producers.name: Cantele
producers.why: A Salento family house near Lecce known for reliable Negroamaro, Primitivo and Chardonnay at fair prices.

producers.name: Taurino
producers.why: A Guagnano estate whose Patriglione, a Negroamaro from partly dried grapes, became an early cult red of the Salento.

producers.name: Polvanera
producers.why: A Gioia del Colle estate on the Murge whose numbered Primitivo bottlings show the fresher, higher altitude side of the grape.

producers.name: Felline (Accademia dei Racemi)
producers.why: The Manduria group of the 1990s that championed old bush vine Primitivo and revived forgotten local grapes such as Susumaniello.

producers.name: Cantine San Marzano
producers.why: The large co-operative of the Manduria zone whose Sessantanni old vine Primitivo carried the DOC to export markets.

terroir.climate: Hot, dry Mediterranean, the sunniest and one of the driest regions of Italy, with rain concentrated in winter and summers that run past 35 degrees. The saving graces are wind and water: breezes from the Adriatic on one side and the Ionian on the other cross the narrow Salento, and the Murge plateau's modest altitude cools the nights at Gioia del Colle and Castel del Monte. Drought is the hazard; irrigation is now allowed and used.
terroir.soils: Limestone underlies the whole region, and over it lies terra rossa, the iron rich red clay that colours the Salento and the Murge; sand along the Ionian coast at Manduria; calcareous tufo and thin stony soils on the Murge; deeper alluvial soils on the Tavoliere plain in the north.
terroir.topography: The flattest region in Italy: the Tavoliere plain of Foggia, the Gargano promontory, the long limestone plateau of the Murge running down the middle at 300 to 500 metres, the Valle d'Itria of trulli houses, and the Salento peninsula, almost at sea level between the Adriatic and the Ionian. Hardly a vineyard rises above 500 metres.
terroir.water: Two seas: the Adriatic on the east and the Ionian in the gulf of Taranto to the west, with the Salento a narrow bridge between them. The Ofanto in the north is the one river of size; the rest of the region drinks from aqueducts, and the vineyards rely on the sea breezes for cool.

traps: Primitivo di Manduria DOC is dry; the DOCG with the same name is Dolce Naturale, the sweet one. Say which you mean.
Negroamaro means black bitter, or black black by another reading; it is not Aglianico and not Nero d'Avola.
Nero di Troia is a Puglian grape most likely named for the town of Troia near Foggia; Homer's Troy is a legend, not a provenance.
Tribidrag is Primitivo under its oldest Croatian name, not its parent; the older course note was loose. The parent idea belongs to Plavac Mali, Tribidrag's child.
Castel del Monte Bombino Nero is a DOCG for rosato alone, the only one in Italy; do not file it with the reds.
Primitivo ripens first, which is what the name means; it is not a primitive or ancient vine in any special sense.
Salice Salentino is a village and a DOC in the Salento; Salento itself is the peninsula and an IGT.
Puglia makes mostly red and rosato; its white Locorotondo is a Verdeca wine, not a Fiano.

wines.note: Deep, ripe and warm, blackberry jam, dried fig, cocoa and sweet spice at fourteen per cent and more, with soft tannin and a plush finish; the Riserva takes two years. Lamb, grilled sausages, aubergine parmigiana, or the cheese course.
The DOCG: Primitivo from late picked or dried bunches fermented to a sweet, strong red of prune and chocolate, poured in a small glass with chocolate or aged cheese.
Primitivo from the Murge plateau at around 300 to 500 metres: fresher, less jammy and more savoury than Manduria, with sour cherry and firmer acidity from the cool nights on limestone.
Negroamaro led with Malvasia Nera: dark plum, dried herbs, a bitter chocolate edge and soft grip, the Riserva after two years. Orecchiette with turnip tops and sausage, lamb and roasted peppers.

Negroamaro bled off its skins after a night's contact, deep coral and dry with cherry and bitter orange; Italy's oldest bottled rosato tradition, from 1943, and the region's best match for its fish and vegetable table.
A DOCG of structured, violet scented red from the Murge around the Swabian castle, firmer and longer lived than the Salento reds, with two years of ageing.

wines.note: A pale, dry rosato DOCG from the Bombino Nero grape, the only DOCG in Italy given to a rosato alone; light cherry and citrus, for the aperitivo and the antipasti.
A light, dry white of Verdeca and Bianco d'Alessano from the Valle d'Itria, neutral and crisp, the trulli country's wine with fresh burrata and raw seafood.

exam: Cannonau is Grenache (Garnacha); Cannonau di Sardegna DOC asks 85 per cent, Riserva two years, with Classico, Jerzu, Oliena and Capo Ferrato as sub-zones.
Vermentino di Gallura is the island's only DOCG (1996), 95 per cent Vermentino on granite in the north east; Vermentino di Sardegna is the DOC everywhere else.
Carignano del Sulcis: Carignan on ungrafted bush vines in the sand of the south west, DOC 1977; Terre Brune as the benchmark.
Vernaccia di Oristano: the island's first DOC (1971), a flor aged, sherry like dry white of 15 per cent, nothing to do with Vernaccia di San Gimignano.
Spanish rule from the fourteenth to the eighteenth century explains the grapes: Cannonau, Carignano, Monica, Bovale, Torbato.
Turriga as the famous IGT blend; Isola dei Nuraghi as the IGT name; Sella & Mosca and Argiolas as the two houses that modernised the island.
The geography: granite in the Gallura, sand in the Sulcis, the Gennargentu mountains, the Campidano plain, the maestrale wind, Corsica across the strait.

grapes.name: Grenache / Garnacha
grapes.styles: Cannonau on this island: the signature red, warm, herbal and high in alcohol with red fruit and soft tannin, from the mountains of Nuoro and Ogliastra at its best; Cannonau di Sardegna DOC covers the whole island.

grapes.name: Vermentino
grapes.styles: The white of the island, saline and citrus scented with a bitter almond finish; Vermentino di Gallura on granite is the DOCG and the fullest, Vermentino di Sardegna the lighter DOC everywhere else.

grapes.name: Carignan
grapes.styles: Carignano in the Sulcis of the south west, grown as old ungrafted bush vines on coastal sand: dark, savoury, plum and dried herb with soft tannin, and far finer than the grape's reputation in France.

grapes.name: Monica
grapes.styles: A soft, light, everyday red said to be Spanish in origin, Monica di Sardegna DOC, drunk young and often blended.

grapes.name: Bovale
grapes.styles: Two grapes under one name, Bovale Sardo and Bovale Grande, thought to have come from Spain, that give colour and tannin to blends such as Turriga and Mandrolisai.

grapes.name: Vernaccia di Oristano
grapes.styles: A white of the Tirso plain unrelated to Tuscany's Vernaccia, aged for years under flor in old chestnut and oak casks into a dry, nutty, sherry like wine of at least fifteen per cent.

grapes.name: Nuragus
grapes.styles: An ancient white of the Cagliari plain, perhaps Phoenician, neutral and crisp; Nuragus di Cagliari DOC.

grapes.name: Torbato
grapes.styles: A white grown almost only around Alghero, Tourbat in Roussillon, for a dry, mineral white and a sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Nasco
grapes.styles: A Cagliari white for sweet and dry wines with a musky, honeyed scent.

grapes.name: Malvasia di Sardegna
grapes.styles: The Malvasia of Bosa on the west coast, made dry under flor or sweet, in the same flor tradition as Vernaccia di Oristano.

law.classification: Sardinia has one DOCG, Vermentino di Gallura, a DOC since 1975 and raised in 1996 for whites of at least 95 per cent Vermentino from the granite of the north east, with a Superiore tier. The island wide DOCs are the ones a server meets: Cannonau di Sardegna (1972), at least 85 per cent Cannonau with the Classico, Capo Ferrato, Jerzu and Oliena (Nepente di Oliena) sub-zones and a Riserva after two years; Vermentino di Sardegna; Monica di Sardegna; Moscato di Sardegna. The local DOCs are Carignano del Sulcis (1977) in the south west, Vernaccia di Oristano, the island's first DOC in 1971, Malvasia di Bosa, Alghero on the north west coast, home of the Sella & Mosca estate, Mandrolisai for a Bovale, Cannonau and Monica blend of the centre, and the Cagliari family of Nuragus, Nasco, Girò, Malvasia and Moscato di Cagliari. Isola dei Nuraghi IGT covers the island and carries the famous barrique aged blends.

At least 85 per cent Cannonau from anywhere on the island; Riserva two years of ageing; sub-zones Classico (the Nuoro and Ogliastra mountains), Capo Ferrato, Jerzu and Oliena; also rosato, passito and liquoroso. DOC 1972.
Carignano del Sulcis DOC
At least 85 per cent Carignano from the Sulcis coast and islands of the south west; Superiore, Riserva after two years, rosato, novello and passito. DOC 1977.
Vernaccia di Oristano DOC

made.viticulture: The island's old vineyard is the alberello, the bush vine, which suits the wind and the drought: in the Sulcis the Carignano stands on its own roots in deep coastal sand that phylloxera could not cross, some of it a century old, and at Mamoiada the Cannonau grows as bush vines on granite sand at 600 to 700 metres. Newer plantings are spur pruned cordon and Guyot, and irrigation is common on the Campidano plain. The maestrale dries the canopy and keeps rot and mildew away, so spraying is light and organic farming easy; the same wind and the summer drought keep yields low without effort. Cannonau is harvested in September and reaches high sugar quickly, so growers in the mountains rely on altitude and cold nights to hold acidity. Vermentino in the Gallura is picked early to keep its bite. Vernaccia di Oristano grows on the flat alluvial gravel of the Tirso, where the vines are cropped for ripeness and the wine is left to the cellar. Co-operatives founded in the mid twentieth century still make a large share of the island's wine, Santadi, Gallura, Jerzu and Dorgali among them.
made.winemaking: Cannonau is made as a warm, soft red: a short to medium maceration, ageing in large old casks or cement for the DOC, and barrique for the Riserva and the IGT blends; the old sweet and fortified Cannonau, Anghelu Ruju among them, is made from dried grapes in the Alghero tradition. Carignano del Sulcis takes longer maceration and a year or two in oak for the Superiore and Riserva, with the Terre Brune of the Santadi co-operative, from 1984, as the model. Vermentino is cool fermented in steel and bottled young, the Gallura DOCG often with a few months on the lees for weight; a Superiore reaches thirteen per cent or more. Vernaccia di Oristano is the island's curiosity: fully fermented, then left for years in old chestnut and oak casks not filled to the top, where a film of flor yeast grows as in Jerez and gives the nutty, dry, oxidative character; the Riserva spends four years and a liquoroso version is fortified. Malvasia di Bosa is made the same way or as a sweet passito. Torbato at Alghero is made still and sparkling.

places.name: Gallura
places.note: The granite north east around Tempio Pausania and the Costa Smeralda, windy and bright, where Vermentino gives the island's only DOCG; the co-operative Cantina di Gallura and the Capichera estate of Arzachena are its names.

places.name: Nuoro, Mamoiada and the Ogliastra
places.note: The mountainous east, the Classico zone of Cannonau di Sardegna: Mamoiada's old bush vines on granite at 600 to 700 metres, Oliena's Nepente, Dorgali, and Jerzu in the Ogliastra with its own sub-zone and co-operative.

places.name: Mamoiada
places.note: A Barbagia village of masked carnival and old alberello Cannonau, whose small growers make some of the island's most structured Cannonau.

places.name: Sulcis
places.note: The south western lowlands and islands around Santadi and Sant'Antioco, where Carignano stands ungrafted in coastal sand and the Santadi co-operative's Terre Brune and Rocca Rubia set the standard; Carignano del Sulcis DOC since 1977.

places.name: Oristano and the Tirso
places.note: The west coast plain and lagoons at the mouth of the Tirso, home of Vernaccia di Oristano, the flor aged white that was Sardinia's first DOC in 1971; Cabras is the village of its reference house, Contini.

places.name: Cagliari and the Campidano
places.note: The southern capital and the hot plain behind it: Nuragus, Nasco, Monica and Malvasia under the Cagliari DOCs, and Serdiana, the village of Argiolas, maker of Turriga.

places.name: Alghero
places.note: The Catalan speaking town of the north west, with the Sella & Mosca estate founded in 1899, Torbato as its own white, the sweet Anghelu Ruju Cannonau and a Cabernet that proved the island could make it.

places.name: Bosa and the Planargia
places.note: The west coast hills above Bosa for the rare Malvasia di Bosa, dry under flor or sweet.

producers.name: Argiolas
producers.why: The Serdiana estate of 1938 whose Turriga, a Cannonau led barrique blend first made in 1988, is the island's most famous red, with Costera Cannonau and Is Argiolas Vermentino beneath it.

producers.name: Sella & Mosca
producers.why: The Alghero estate founded in 1899 by two Piedmontese, long the island's largest, with Torbato Terre Bianche, the Marchese di Villamarina Cabernet and the sweet Anghelu Ruju Cannonau.

producers.name: Attilio Contini
producers.why: The Cabras family house of 1898 whose Antico Gregori solera is the reference Vernaccia di Oristano.

producers.name: Cantina Santadi
producers.why: The Sulcis co-operative whose Terre Brune of 1984 and Rocca Rubia turned ungrafted bush vine Carignano into a serious red.

producers.name: Capichera
producers.why: The Arzachena estate in the Gallura that made Vermentino a wine of weight and ageing, with a barrel aged version, long sold outside the DOCG as IGT.

producers.name: Cantina di Gallura
producers.why: The Tempio Pausania co-operative founded in 1956 and a leading name in Vermentino di Gallura, with Canayli as its Superiore.

producers.name: Giuseppe Sedilesu
producers.why: The Mamoiada estate, named for a founder of the 1970s, that put the village's old bush vine Cannonau on the map with Mamuthone.

producers.name: Cantina Sociale di Jerzu
producers.why: The Ogliastra co-operative of 1950 behind the Jerzu sub-zone of Cannonau di Sardegna.

producers.name: Tenute Dettori
producers.why: A Sennori estate in the north working old Cannonau and Vermentino vines without additions, the island's natural wine reference.
